  "passage_text": "Again in the Sabazian mysteries, which some connect with Dionysus and
others with Zeus, the little that is known of the ritual favours the
view that here also the _motif_ was the marriage of the deity with his
worshippers. According to Clement[1469], the subject-matter of these
mysteries was a story that Zeus, having become by Demeter the father
of Persephone, seduced in turn his own daughter, having as a means to
that end transformed himself into a snake. That story, it may safely be
said, is presented by Clement in its worst light; but the statement,
that in the ritual the deity was represented by a snake, obtains some
corroboration from Theophrastus, who says of the superstitious man,
that if he see a red snake in his house he will invoke Sabazius[1470].
Now the token of these mysteries for those who were being initiated
in them was, according to Clement[1471] again, ‘the god pressed to
the bosom’ (ὁ διὰ κόλπου θεός); which phrase he explains by saying
that the god was represented as a snake, which was passed under the
clothing and drawn over the bosom of the initiated ‘as a proof of the
incontinence of Zeus.’ Clearly then the act of initiation was the
symbolic wedding of the worshipper with the deity worshipped; and it is
probable that the union which was symbolized in this life was expected
to be realised in the next.

Finally in the orgiastic worship of Cybele the same religious doctrine
is revealed. Here to Attis seems to be assigned the same part as to
Adonis in the mysteries of Aphrodite. He is the beloved of the goddess;
he is lost and mourned for as dead; he is restored again from the
grave to the goddess who loved him. And in all this he appears to be
the representative of all Cybele’s worshippers; for the ritual of
initiation into her rites, if once again we may avail ourselves of
Clement’s statements, is strongly imbued with the idea of marriage
between the goddess and her worshipper. The several acts or stages of
initiation are summarised in four phrases: ‘I ate out of the drum; I
drank out of the cymbal; I carried the sacred vessel; I entered privily
the bed-chamber--ἐκ τυμπάνου ἔφαγον· ἐκ κυμβάλου ἔπιον· ἐκερνοφόρησα·
ὑπὸ τὸν παστὸν ὑπέδυν[1472]. In the passage from which these phrases
are culled there appears to be a certain confusion between the rites
of Cybele and those of Demeter; but the fact that Clement shortly
afterwards gives another formulary of Demeter’s ritual is sufficient
proof that he meant this present formulary, as indeed the mention of
kettle-drum and cymbal[1473] suggests, to apply to the mysteries of
Cybele[1474]. It appears then that the final act or stage of initiation
consisted in the secret admission of the worshipper to the bed-chamber
of the goddess. Such ritual can have borne only one interpretation. It
clearly constituted a promise of wedded union between the initiated
and their deity. Viewed in this light even the emasculation of the
priests of Cybele may more readily be understood; it may have been the
consecration of their virility to the service of the goddess, a final
and convincing pledge of celibacy in this life, in return for which
they aspired to be blest by wedlock with their goddess hereafter.

The mention of the goddess’ bed-chamber in the above passage is of
considerable interest. The παστός (or παστάς) in relation to a temple
meant the same thing as it often meant in relation to an ordinary
house, an inner room or recess screened off, and in particular a
bridal chamber. Such provision for the physical comfort of the deity
was probably not rare. Pausanias tells us that on the right of
the vestibule in the Argive Heraeum there was a couch (κλίνη) for
Hera[1475], and he seems to speak of it as if it were a common enough
piece of temple furniture. So too at Phlya in Attica, where were held
the very ancient mystic rites ‘of her who is called the Great,’ there
was a bridal chamber (παστάς), where, it has rightly been argued, there
‘must have been enacted a mimetic marriage[1476].’ Again Clement of
Alexandria speaks of a παστός of Athena in the Parthenon, and makes
it quite clear by the story which he relates that he understood the
word in the sense of bed-chamber. The story is also for other reasons
worth recalling, because it shows how the religious conception of
marriage between men and gods was readily extended to the worship of
other deities than those whose mysteries we have sought to unravel,
and at the same time furnishes the only case known to me in which
that mystic belief was prostituted to the base uses of flattery. The
occasion was the reception accorded by the Athenians to Demetrius
Poliorcetes. Not content with hailing him as a god in name, they went
so far in their mean-spirited subjection as to set up a temple, at
the place where he dismounted from his horse on entering their city,
to Demetrius the Descender (Καταιβάτης)[1477], while on every side
altars were erected to him. But their grossest piece of flattery was
a master-piece of grotesque impiety, and met with a fitting reward. A
marriage was arranged between him (the most notorious profligate of his
age) and Athena. ‘He however,’ we are told, ‘disdained the goddess,
being unable to embrace the statue, but took with him to the Acropolis
the courtesan Lamia, and polluted the bed-chamber of Athena, exhibiting
to the old virgin the postures of the young courtesan[1478].’ Even that
contemptuous response to the Athenians’ flattery did not abash them,
but, finding that he did not favour their acknowledged deity, they
determined to deify his acknowledged favourite, and erected a temple to
Lamia Aphrodite[1479]."
}

  "passage_text": "But such travesties of holy things were rare; and this one notorious
case excited the contempt alike of the man[1480] to whom the flattery
was paid and of all posterity--a contempt which teaches, hardly less
clearly than the indignation excited a century earlier by the supposed
profanation of the mysteries, in what reverence and high esteem the
idea of marriage between men and gods was generally held.

Even Lucian, in whom reverence was a less pronounced characteristic
than humour, condemns seriously enough a parody of the mysteries
of Eleusis which occurred in his own day; and his account of it at
the same time shows once more that the marriage of men and gods was
the very essence of the mysteries. The impostor Alexander, he says,
instituted rites with carrying of torches (δᾳδουχία) and exposition
of the sacred ceremonies (ἱεροφαντία) lasting for three days. “On
the first there was a proclamation, as at Athens, as follows: ‘If
any atheist, Christian, or Epicurean hath come to spy upon the holy
rites, let him begone, and let the faithful be initiated with heaven’s
blessing.’ Then first of all there was an expulsion of intruders.
Alexander himself led the way, crying ‘Out with Christians,’ and the
whole multitude shouted in answer ‘Out with Epicureans.’ Then was
enacted the story of Leto in child-bed and the birth of Apollo, and his
marriage with Coronis and the birth of Asclepius; and on the second day
the manifestation of Glycon and the god’s birth[1481]. And on the third
day was the wedding of Podalirius and Alexander’s mother; this was
called the Torch-day, for torches were burnt. And finally there was the
love of Selene and Alexander, and the birth of his daughter now married
to Rutilianus[1482]. Our Endymion-Alexander was now torch-bearer and
exponent of the rites. And he lay as it were sleeping in the view of
all, and there came down to him from the roof--as it were Selene from
heaven--a certain Rutilia, a very beautiful woman, the wife of one of
Caesar’s household-officers, who was really in love with Alexander
and was loved by him, and she kissed the rascal’s eyes and embraced
him in the view of all, and, if there had not been so many torches,
worse would perhaps have followed (τάχα ἄν τι καὶ τῶν ὑπὸ κόλπου
ἐπράττετο)[1483].”

The inferences which may be drawn from this narrative are, first, that
the mysteries in general, while reproducing in some dramatic form the
whole story of the deities concerned, culminated in the representation
of a mystic marriage between men and gods; (the birth of a child was
also represented or announced in this parody, as we know that it
was at Eleusis[1484], but it had, I am inclined to think, no mystic
significance otherwise than as proof of the consummation of that
marriage;) and, secondly, that the wild charges of indecency brought by
early Christian writers against the mysteries are baseless; for Lucian
condemns a much lesser license in this parody than that which they
attributed to the genuine rites.

Thus our examination of the mysteries, so far as they are known to us,
tends to prove that the doctrines revealed in them to the initiated
were simply a development of certain vaguer popular ideas which have
been prevalent among the Greek folk from the classical age down to our
own day. The people entertained hopes that this physical life would
continue in a similar form after death; the mysteries gave definite
assurance of that immortality by exhibiting to the initiated Persephone
or Adonis or Attis restored from the lower world in bodily form; and
though that exhibition was in fact merely a dramatic representation,
yet to the eyes of religious ecstasy it seemed just as much a living
reality as does the risen Christ in the modern celebration of Easter.
The people again were wont to think and to speak of death as a marriage
into the lower world; the mysteries showed to the initiated certain
representatives of mankind who by death, or even in life, had been
admitted to the felicity of wedlock with deities, and thereby confirmed
the faithful in their happier hopes of being in like manner themselves
god-beloved and of sharing the life of gods.

Since then there is good reason to believe that this was in effect the
secret teaching of the mysteries, it would naturally be expected that
human marriage should have been reckoned as it were a foretaste of
that union with the divine which was promised hereafter, and also that
death should have been counted the hour of its approaching fulfilment;
in other words, if my view of the mysteries is correct, it would
almost inevitably follow that the mysteries should have been brought
into close association both with weddings and with funerals. This
expectation is confirmed by the facts.

An ordinary wedding was treated as something akin to initiation into
the mysteries. An inscription of Cos[1485], relating to the appointment
of priestesses of Demeter, mentions among other duties certain services
on the occasion of weddings; and the brides, who are the recipients
of these services, are divided into two classes, αἱ τελεύμεναι and αἱ
ἐπινυμφευόμεναι, the maidens who, are being ‘initiated,’ and the widows
who are being married again; a woman’s first marriage in fact is called
by a religious document her initiation, and Demeter’s priestesses
are charged therewith. Nor was this usage or idea confined to Cos;
Plutarch speaks of services rendered by the priestess of Demeter in
the solemnisation of matrimony as part of an ‘ancestral rite[1486]’;
while the term τέλος was commonly used both of the mystic rites and of
marriage, and τέλειοι might denote the newly-wed[1487]."
}

  "passage_text": "The same thought seems also to have inspired another custom\nassociated with marriage. The newly-wed, we hear, sometimes attended\na representation of the marriage of Zeus and Hera[1488], an ἱερὸς\nγάμος which formed the subject of mystic drama or legend all over\nGreece[1489]. The widely extended cults of Hera under the titles of\nMaiden (παρθένος or παῖς) and of Bride (τελεία or νυμφευομένη) appear\nto have been closely interwoven; indeed for a full appreciation of the\nGreek conception of the goddess they must be treated as complementary.\nThey are well interpreted by Farnell. Rejecting the theory of physical\nsymbolism, he suggests ‘a more human explanation. Hera was essentially\nthe goddess of women, and the life of women was reflected in her;\ntheir maidenhood and marriage were solemnised by the cults of Hera\nΠαρθένος and Hera Τελεία or Νυμφευομένη, and the very rare worship of\nHera Χήρα might allude to the not infrequent custom of divorce and\nseparation[1490].’ With, Hera the Widow we are not here concerned,\nbut only with the higher conceptions of Zeus and Hera as expressed in\nthe representation of the ‘sacred marriage’; the bride and bridegroom\nwho looked upon that saw in it, we may be sure, not a symbolical\nrepresentation of the seasons and the productive powers of the earth,\nbut rather the divine prototype of human marriage. It reminded them\nthat deities, like mortals, were married and given in marriage, and it\nimparted to their wedding a sacramental character, making it at once a\nforetaste and a gage of that close communion with the gods which, when\ndeath the dividing line between mortals and immortals should once be\npassed, awaited the blessed among mankind.\n\nOther small points too suggest the same trend of thought. The\npreliminaries of a wedding often comprised a sacrifice to Zeus\nTeleios and Hera Teleia[1491], and were called προτέλεια being the\n‘preliminaries of initiation’ into that mystery, of which the\nsacred marriage, enacted before the now wedded pair, was the full\nrevelation[1492]. Again these preliminaries always included the\nsolemn ablution[1493] of which I have spoken above, and in this\nresembled the preparations for admittance to the mysteries. Moreover\nan instance is recorded in which this ablution was itself invested\nwith the significance of a wedding between the human and the divine.\nThe maidens of the Troad before marriage were wont to unrobe and bathe\nthemselves in the Scamander; and the prayer which they made to the\nriver-god, whose bed they entered, was, ‘Receive thou, Scamander, my\nvirginity[1494].’ Finally the first night on which the wedded pair came\ntogether was known as the ‘mystic night’ (νὺξ μυστική)[1495], a term\nnot a little suggestive of the great night of Demeter’s mysteries when\nto the eyes of the initiated was displayed the secret proof and promise\nof wedlock between men and gods hereafter. In short the ceremonies\nof a wedding by one means or another proclaimed it to be a form of\ninitiation, and the estate of marriage was to the Greeks, as our\nprayer-book calls it, ‘an excellent mystery.’"

  "passage_text": "Hence naturally followed the belief that the unmarried and the
uninitiated shared the same fate in the future life. One conception
of the punishment of the uninitiated was, according to Plato[1496],
that they should carry water in a sieve to a broken jar; and this, as
is well known, was also the lot of the Danaids in the nether world.
Commenting on these facts Dr Frazer says, ‘It is possible that the
original reason why the Danaids were believed to be condemned to this
punishment in hell was not so much that they murdered, as that they did
not marry, the sons of Aegyptus. According to one tradition indeed they
afterwards married other husbands (Paus. III. 12. 2); but according
to another legend they were murdered by Lynceus, apparently before
marriage (Schol. on Euripides, _Hecuba_, 886). They may therefore have
been chosen as types of unmarried women, and their punishment need
not have been peculiar to them but may have been the one supposed to
await all unmarried persons in the nether world[1497].’ A passage of
Lucian, which appears to have been overlooked in this connexion[1498],
converts the view of the Danaids which Dr Frazer considers possible
into a practical certainty. The passage in point forms the conclusion
of that dialogue in which Poseidon with the aid of Triton plots and
carries out the rape of Amymone, the Danaid. She has just been seized
and is protesting against her abduction and threatening to call her
father, when Triton intervenes: ‘Keep quiet, Amymone,’ he says, ‘it
is Poseidon.’ And the girl rejoins, ‘Oh, Poseidon you call him, do
you?’ and then turning to her ravisher, ‘What do you mean, sirrah, by
handling me so roughly, and dragging me down into the sea? I shall
go under and be drowned, miserable girl.’ And Poseidon answers, ‘Do
not be frightened, you shall come to no harm; no, I will strike the
rock here, near where the waves break, with my trident, and will let
a spring burst up which shall bear your name, and you yourself shall
be blessed and, unlike your sisters, shall not carry water when you
are dead (καὶ σὺ εὐδαίμων ἔσῃ καὶ μόνη τῶν ἀδελφῶν οὐχ ὑδροφορήσεις
ἀποθανοῦσα)[1499].’ The whole point of Poseidon’s answer clearly
depends upon the existence of a well-known belief that the Danaids were
punished hereafter for remaining unmarried and that the punishment took
the form of vainly fetching water for that bridal bath which was a
necessary preliminary to a wedding; Amymone shall have a very thorough
bridal bath, and the spring that bears her name shall be a monument
of it, while she herself shall be ‘blessed’ by wedlock with Poseidon;
thus shall she escape the fate of the unmarried. Clearly then there was
no distinction between the uninitiated and the unmarried; both alike
were doomed vainly to fetch water for those ablutions which preceded
initiation into the mysteries or into matrimony; and once again the
conception of marriage as a mystic and sacramental rite akin to the
rites of Eleusis is clearly revealed.

It may further be noted here that this idea of the punishment of the
unmarried completely explains the custom, on which I have already
touched, of erecting a water-pitcher (λουτροφόρος) over the grave of
unmarried persons. This intimated, according to Eustathius[1500], that
the person there buried had never taken the bath which both bride and
bridegroom were wont to take before marriage. But this must not be
taken to mean that the water-pitcher was erected as a symbol of the
punishment which the dead person was supposed to be undergoing; this
was not an idea which his relatives and friends, even if they had held
it, would have wished to blazon abroad. One might as soon expect to
find depicted on a modern tombstone the worm that dieth not and the
fire that is not quenched. No; the water-pitcher was not a symbol, it
was an instrument; for my part I have little faith in the existence
of any symbols in popular religion which are not in origin at least
instruments; and the purpose to which this instrument was put was to
supply the dead person with that wedding-bath which he had not taken
in life, and without which he would vainly strive in the under-world
to prepare himself for divine wedlock. The water-pitcher was not
commemorative, but preventive, of future punishment. Its erection was
not a warning to the living, but a service to the dead.

Thus then the evidence for the intimate association of the mysteries,
or of the main idea which runs through them, with human weddings is
complete and, I hope, convincing; and the custom of the water-pitcher,
which concludes it, fitly introduces at the same time the evidence
for the association of the same idea with funerals. This is equally
plentiful. The vague conception of death as a wedding, which as I have
shown was elaborated in the mysteries, has of course already been
exemplified in all those passages of ancient literature and modern
folk-songs which I have adduced, and I have found in it also the motive
for the assimilation of funeral-customs to the customs of marriage.
But the evidence that the actual doctrines of the mysteries, in which
more definite expression was given to that vague idea, were closely
associated with death and funeral-custom is to be found rather in
epitaphs and sepulchral monuments.
The tone of the epitaphs may be sufficiently illustrated by a single
couplet:

    Οὐκ ἐπιδὼν νύμφεια λέχη κατέβην τὸν ἄφυκτον
      Γόργιππος ξανθῆς Φερσεφόνης θάλαμον[1501]."
}

  "passage_text": "‘I, Gorgippus, lived not to look upon a bridal bed ere I went down
to the chamber of bright-haired Persephone which none may escape.’
There is naturally here a note of lament, as befits any epitaph, and
more especially that of one who dies young and unmarried; but none
the less there is an anticipation--justified, we may think, if we
will, by some ceremony of bridal ablution performed for the dead man
by his friends--that his death is a wedding with the goddess of the
under-world; and indeed the phrase Φερσεφόνης θάλαμος, ‘the bridal
chamber of Persephone,’ recurs with some frequency in this class of
epitaphs[1502].

Considered collectively, such epitaphs would suggest a distinctly
offensive conception of Persephone; but in each taken separately, as
it was composed, it will be allowed, I think, that if there is supreme
audacity, there is equal sublimity. It is just these qualities which
give pungency to a blasphemous parody of such epitaphs, in which the
wit of Ausonius exposes the worst possible aspect of a religious
conception which to the pure-minded was wholly pure. My apology for
quoting lines which I will not translate must be the fact that a
caricature is often no less instructive than a true portrait. The mock
epitaph concludes as follows:

    Sed neque functorum socius miscebere vulgo
      Nec metues Stygios flebilis umbra lacus:
    Verum aut Persephonae Cinyreius ibis Adonis,
      Aut Jovis Elysii tu catamitus eris[1503].

Ausonius in jest bears an unpleasant resemblance to Clement in earnest;
both perverted to their uttermost a doctrine which commanded nothing
but reverence from faithful participants in the mysteries.

Akin to these epitaphs are certain tablets which recently have been
fully discussed by Miss Jane Harrison[1504], and have been shown to
be of Orphic origin. They were buried with the dead, and for this
reason were more outspoken in their references to the mystic doctrines
than was permissible in epitaphs exposed to the vulgar gaze. The most
complete of these tablets is one which was found near Sybaris, and,
with the exception of the last sentence of all, the inscription is in
hexameter verse. Miss Harrison, to whose work I am wholly indebted for
this valuable evidence, translates as follows[1505]:

    ‘Out of the pure I come, Pure Queen of Them Below,
    Eukles and Eubouleus and the other Gods immortal.
    For I also avow me that I am of your blessed race,
    But Fate laid me low and the other Gods immortal
                              ... starflung thunderbolt.
    I have flown out of the sorrowful weary Wheel.
    I have passed with eager feet to the Circle desired.
    I have sunk beneath the bosom of Despoina, Queen of the Underworld.
    I have passed with eager feet from the Circle desired.
    Happy and Blessed One, thou shalt be God instead of mortal.
            A kid I have fallen into milk.’

The gist of the document which the dead man takes with him is then
briefly this. He claims to have been pure originally and of the same
race as his gods; but as a man he was mortal and exposed to death,
and in this respect differed from his gods. He states however that he
has performed certain ritual acts which entitle him to be re-admitted
to the pure fellowship of the gods now that death is passed. And the
answer comes, ‘Thou shalt be God instead of mortal.’

Now here I wish to consider one only of these ritual acts--that one of
which the meaning is clearest--Δεσποίνας δ’ ὑπὸ κόλπον ἔδυν χθονίας
βασιλείας, which means, if I may give my own rendering, ‘I was admitted
to the embrace of Despoina, Queen of the under-world.’ The phrase
is one which repeats the idea which we have already seen expressed
in the formulary of Cybele’s rites, ὑπὸ τὸν παστὸν ὑπέδυν[1506], ‘I
was privily admitted to the bridal chamber,’ and in the token of the
Sabazian mysteries, ὁ διὰ κόλπου θεός[1507], ‘the god pressed to
the bosom’; and Lucian’s final phrase in his account of Alexander’s
mock-mysteries shows a kindred phrase, τὰ ὑπὸ κόλπου[1508], as an
euphemism of the same kind[1509]. The Orphic therefore no less than
others based his claim to future happiness on the fact that he had
performed a ritual act, of the nature of a sacrament, which constituted
a pledge that the wedlock between him and his goddess foreshadowed here
should be consummated hereafter.

Even more abundant evidence is furnished by sepulchral monuments;
and in support of my views I cannot do better than quote two high
authorities who coincide in their verdict upon the meaning of the
scenes represented. In reference to those scenes ‘in which death
is conceived in the guise of a marriage’ Furtwängler writes: ‘The
monuments belonging to this class are extraordinarily numerous, and
exhibit very different methods of treating the idea which they carry
out. A relief upon a sarcophagus from the Villa Borghese shows the God
of the dead in the act of carrying down the fair Kore to be his bride
in the lower world. Above the steeds of his chariot, which are already
disappearing into the depths of the earth, flies Eros as guide. The
bride however appears to be going only under compulsion and after some
struggle; the look of the bridegroom expresses sternness rather than
gentleness; and the mother who sits with face averted seems to exclude
all thoughts of the daughter’s return. Only in the torches which the
guide carries in his hand, in the snakes which are looking upward, and
in the observant attitude of Hecate, can a suggestion of the return be
found.

‘On another sarcophagus--from Nazzara--which represents the same
marriage-journey, Eros is not merely the guide of the steeds, but aids
the bridegroom in carrying off Kore, so that in this case the struggle
with death takes purely the form of a struggle with love. At the same
time the mother is driving along with her chariot, thereby signifying
the renewal of life, which is yet more clearly betokened in the
ploughman and the sower at her side."
}

Here there is a look of gentleness\non Hades’ face; the bride accompanies him gladly, and even takes an\naffectionate farewell of her mother, who appears to acquiesce in her\ndeparture. In this case too Eros is flying above the horses, and is\nturned towards the lovers, while in front of him there flies a dove,\nthe bird sacred to the goddess of love. Hecate with torches guides the\nsteeds; near at hand waits Hermes to escort the procession; and above\nthe whole scene the stars are shining, as if to indicate the new life\nin the region of death.\n\n‘In another form, exalted to a yet higher holiness, the same marriage\nis repeated in the sphere of Dionysus-worship. Thus on a cameo in the\nVatican, Dionysus is represented driving with his bride, Ariadne, in\na brightly-decked triumphal car. Holy rapture is manifested on the\nfeatures of both, and on top of the chariot stands a Cupid directing\nit. Dionysus is arrayed in the doe-skin, and holds in his left hand\na _thyrsus_, in his right a goblet; Ariadne is carrying ears of corn\nand poppy-heads, and has her hair wreathed with vine-leaves. The car\nis drawn by Centaurs of both sexes, with torches, drinking-horns,\nand musical instruments. The idea which underlies this scene is the\nreproduction of Life out of Death; Hades has issued forth again for\na new marriage-bond with Kore in the realm of light, appearing now\nrejuvenated in the form of Dionysus, just as his bride assumes the form\nof Ariadne, and because the power of death is broken behind him, his\ncar likewise becomes a triumphal car.\n\n‘Just as the marriage of Zeus in the realm of light became a type for\nmen in this life, so the marriage of Hades, or of Dionysus representing\nhim, developed into a similar prototype for the dead. Since that which\nis true of Death bears directly upon the actual dead, it was quite\nnatural that gradually the process of death came to be considered in\ngeneral as a wedding with the deities of death. With this conception\ntoo harmonize those wedding-scenes which are so common and conspicuous\non funeral monuments, as well as the often-recurring scenes from the\njoyous cycle of Dionysus-myths[1510].’\nTwo brief comments may be made upon this passage. First, Furtwängler\nclearly recognises in Dionysus a mere substitute for Hades, and thus\nconfirms my interpretation of the strange legend concerning Dionysus\nand Prosymnus[1511]. We noticed that the somewhat obscure observation\nof Heraclitus (as quoted by Clement) upon that story contained the\nwords ‘Dionysus and Hades are one and the same’; and we now see that\nin art too the same identification was made, and that the marriage of\na mortal with Dionysus was used to typify the future marriage of the\ndead with their gods. The reason for this identification seems simply\nto be that the cults in which the two gods figured, although differing\nin outward form, were felt to express one and the same idea--namely the\nconception of death as a form of marriage; and the tendency to identify\nin such cases was carried so far that the god Dionysus was even, we are\ntold, identified with the mortal Adonis[1512], presumably because the\nworship of each, as I have shown above, turned upon this one cardinal\ndoctrine.\n\nSecondly, Furtwängler points out that the marriage of Zeus and Hera\nrepresented for living men the same doctrine as the marriage of Hades\nand Persephone (or of Dionysus and Ariadne) represented for the dead.\nThe truth of this is well illustrated by the close resemblance between\nAristophanes’ picture of Hera’s wedding and those funeral monuments\nand vases which Furtwängler describes; for there too ‘golden-winged\nEros held firm the reins, and drave the wedding-car of Zeus and blessed\nHera[1513].’ In other words, this Olympian marriage was only one among\nseveral mystic marriages which all conveyed, though in diverse form,\nthe same lesson, that marriage was the perfection of divine life no\nless than of human life, and therefore that hereafter when men, or at\nany rate the blessed and initiated among men, should come to dwell with\ntheir gods, no bond of communion between gods and men could be perfect\nshort of the marriage-bond."
}

  "passage_text": "It was natural enough that the drama of Hera’s wedding with Zeus should\nmost often have been chosen to be played at an ordinary wedding,\nbecause it would not obtrude thoughts of death upon a joyous event\nwith such insistence as most of the other religious legends which\nreposed upon the same fundamental doctrine; but sometimes, we know, it\nwas the priestesses of Demeter who officiated at wedding-ceremonies,\nand in those cases it cannot be doubted that it was Persephone and not\nHera who was the divine prototype of the bride, and the thought that\nher wedding was a wedding with the god of death could not have been\nexcluded. At funerals, on the other hand, the story of Zeus and Hera\nwhich was preferred at weddings owing to its less obvious allusion to\ndeath, would for that same reason have found less favour than those\nother marriage-legends in which the identity of death with marriage\nwas more clearly enunciated; and of these, owing to the exceptional\nreverence in which the Eleusinian mysteries were held, the story of\nPersephone seems to have been among the most frequent. Yet in the\npicture drawn by Aristophanes at which we have just glanced, for one\nsubtle touch which suggests the connexion of Hera’s wedding with human\nweddings, there is another subtle touch which suggests its relation\nwith human death. The first is an epithet applied to Eros who drove the\nwedding-car--the epithet ἀμφιθαλής, used of one who has both parents\nliving[1514]. The allusion to human weddings is clear. It was no doubt\nimperative in old time, as it still is, in Greece, that anyone who\nattended upon a bride or bridegroom, as for instance the bearer of\nwater for the bridal bath, should have both parents living; and the\nuse of the same term in reference to Eros, the attendant upon Zeus\nand Hera, marks the intimate connexion between the divine marriage\nand the marriage of living men and women. But another epithet in the\npassage conveys no less clear an allusion to the marriage of those,\nwhom men call dead, with their deities. Hera is named εὐδαίμων, a word\nwhich, meaning ‘favoured by God,’ may seem strangely applied to one\nwho herself was divine[1515]. But it was selected by Aristophanes for\na good reason; by the word εὐδαιμονία was commonly denoted that future\nbliss which the initiated believed to consist in wedlock with their\ndeities. Like θεοφιλής, ‘god-beloved,’ the term εὐδαίμων, ‘blessed,’\nwas, so to speak, a catch-word of the mysteries[1516]; and the\napplication of it to Hera in Aristophanes’ ode brings the legend of\nHera’s marriage into rank with those other wedding-stories whose actual\nplot hinged upon the identity of death and marriage. Thus though one\nlegend might be more appropriate in its externals to one occasion, and\nanother legend to another occasion, the ultimate and fundamental idea\nof them all was single and the same.\n\nThis view is boldly championed by the second authority whom I proposed\nto quote upon the subject of mystic marriage-scenes depicted on\nfuneral-monuments. ‘The idea,’ says Lenormant, ‘of mystic union\nin death is frequently indicated in the scenes represented upon\n_sarcophagi_ and painted vases. But for the most part the idea is\nexpressed there only in an allusive manner, which depends upon the\nidentification which this marriage-scene established between the dead\nperson and the deity, by means of such subjects as the carrying off\nof Cephalus by Aurora, or Orithyia by Boreas, or the love-story of\nAphrodite and Adonis[1517].’ ‘Thus,’ he explains, ‘a girl carried\noff (by death) from her parents was simply a bride betrothed to the\ninfernal god, and was identified with Demeter’s maiden daughter, the\nvictim of the passion and violence of Hades; a young man cut off by an\nearly fate figured as the beautiful Adonis, snatched away by Persephone\nfrom the love of Aphrodite, and brought, in spite of himself, to the\nbed of the queen of the lower world[1518].’ The identification which\nLenormant sees in these several instances is an identification, I\nsuppose, not of personalities but of destinies. The popular religion\nof ancient Greece shows little trace of any pantheistic view which\nwould have contemplated the absorption of the personality of the dead\nman or woman into that of any god or goddess. Indeed the very number\nof the personally distinct deities with whom, on such an hypothesis,\nthe dead would have been identified, as well as that continuance of\nsexual difference in the future life which is postulated by the very\ndoctrine before us, precludes all thought of personal identification.\nRather it is the future destiny of the dead person which was identified\nwith the destiny of the deity or hero whose marriage was represented on\nsarcophagus or _cippus_ or commemorative vase[1519]. The lot of Kore or\nAriadne or Orithyia prefigured the lot of mortal women hereafter; the\nfortunes of Adonis or Cephalus typified those of mortal men; and all\nthe marriage-scenes alike, whatever the differences of presentation,\nrevealed the hope and the promise of wedlock hereafter between mankind\nand their deities."
}

  "passage_text": "But Lenormant mentions one vase-painting[1520] in which this
fundamental doctrine is taught not by parables of mythology, but more
overtly and directly. The scene depicted is the marriage of a youth,
whose name, Polyetes, is in pathetic contrast with his short span of
years spent upon earth, with a goddess Eudaemonia (or ‘Bliss’) in the
lower world. In this deity Lenormant sees ‘the infernal goddess under
an euphemistic name.’ Nor could any more significant name have been
used. It has already been pointed out that εὐδαιμονία was a term much
favoured by the initiated in the mysteries, and was openly used by them
to denote that future bliss which secretly was understood to consist in
divine wedlock. Hence the scene upon this vase would at once suggest to
those who were familiar with the doctrines of the mysteries, that the
youth, being presumably of the number of the initiated, had found in
death the realisation of his happy hopes and had entered into blissful
union with the goddess of the lower world.

       *       *       *       *       *

To sum up briefly: we have seen alike in the literature of ancient
Greece and in the folk-songs of modern Greece that death has commonly
been conceived by the Hellenic race in the guise of a wedding; a review
of marriage-customs and funeral-customs both ancient and modern has
re-affirmed the constant association of death and marriage, and has
shown how deep-rooted in the minds of the common people that idea must
have been which produced a deliberate assimilation of funeral-rites
to the ceremonies of marriage. Next we investigated the connexion
of the mysteries with the popular religion, and saw reason to hold
that, far from being subversive of it or alien to it, they inculcated
doctrines which were wholly evolved from vaguer popular ideas always
current in Greece. Finally we traced in many of those legends, on which
the dramatic representations of the mysteries are known to have been
based, a common _motif_, the idea that death is the entrance for men
into a blissful estate of wedded union with their deities. And this
religious ideal not only satisfies the condition of agreement with,
and evolution from, those popular views in which death figured somewhat
vaguely as a form of wedding, but also proves to be the natural and
necessary outcome of two religious sentiments with which earlier
chapters have dealt; first, the ardent desire for close communion with
the gods, and secondly, the belief that men’s bodies as well as their
souls survived death and dissolution; for if the body by means of its
disintegration rejoined the soul in the nether world, and the human
entity was then complete, enjoying the same substantial existence,
the same physical no less than mental powers, which it had enjoyed in
the upper world, and which the immortal gods enjoyed uninterrupted by
death, then, since the same rite of marriage was the consummation both
of divine life and of human life, men’s yearning for close communion
with their gods required for its ideal and perfect satisfaction the
full union of wedlock; and the sacrament which assured men of this
consummation was the highest development of the whole Greek religion,
the mysteries.

Such a sacrament and such aspirations might well have offended even
those Christians of early days, if such there were, who were willing to
deal sympathetically with paganism; that those who were its declared
enemies, and were ready to use against it the weapons of perversion and
vituperation, found in this conception a vulnerable point, is readily
understood. It is true indeed that in the very idea which they most
vilified there was a certain curious analogy between the new religion
and the old. Just as paganism allowed to each man or woman individually
the hope of becoming the bridegroom or the bride of one of their many
deities, so Christianity represented the Church, the whole body of the
faithful collectively, as the bride of its sole deity. But the analogy
is superficial only. The bond of feeling which united the Church with
God was very differently conceived from that which drew together the
pagans and their deities. The chastened ‘charity’ (ἀγάπη) of the
Christians had little in common with the passionate love (ἔρως) with
which the Greeks of old time had dared look upon their gods. Theirs
was the Love that ‘held firm the reins and drave the wedding-car of
Zeus and blessed Hera[1521]’; the Love that hovered above the steeds
of Hades and changed for Persephone the road of death into a road to
bliss; the Love whom ‘no immortal may escape nor any of mankind whose
life passeth it as a day, but whoso hath him is as one mad[1522]’; and
the only true consummation of such love was wedlock.

This conception necessarily implied the equality of men with their gods
in the future life; and that future equality was sometimes represented
as no more than a return to that which was in the beginning. ‘One is
the race of men with the race of gods; for one is the mother that gave
to both our breath; yet are they sundered by powers wholly diverse, in
that mankind is as naught, but heaven is builded of brass that abideth
ever unshaken[1523].’ So sang Pindar of the past and of the present;
but the Orphic tablet which has been already quoted carries on the
thought into the future:

    ‘Out of the pure I come, Pure Queen of Them Below,
    Eukles and Eubouleus and the other Gods immortal.
    For I also avow me that I am of your blessed race,
    But Fate laid me low....’

So far with Pindar. But the dead man’s claims do not end there: ‘I was
admitted to the embrace of Despoina, Queen of the Underworld’; already
had he received a foretaste of that divine wedlock which implied
equality with the gods; and so there comes the answer, ‘Happy and
Blessed One, thou shalt be God instead of mortal.’"
}

  "passage_text": "This idea commended itself even to thinkers who did not believe in\nbodily survival after death. Plato, in the _Phaedo_, where above all\nthings is taught the perishable nature of the body and the immortality\nof the soul alone, yet avails himself of the belief that the pure among\nmankind shall attain even to godhead hereafter. To him the pure are\nnot the initiated indeed, but the earnest strivers after wisdom. In\nhis theory of retributive metempsychosis he surmises that those who\nhave followed the lusts of the flesh shall hereafter enter the ranks of\nasses and other lustful beasts; that those who have wrought violence\nshall enter the ranks of wolves and hawks and kites; that those who\nhave practised what is popularly accounted virtue, but without true\nunderstanding, shall enter the ranks of harmless and social creatures,\nbees, wasps, and ants, or even the ranks of men once more. ‘But\ninto the ranks of gods none may enter without having followed after\nwisdom and so departing hence wholly pure--none save the lover of\nknowledge[1524].’ What precise meaning Plato attached to his phrase\n‘to enter the ranks’ (εἰς γένος ἐνδύεσθαι or ἀφικνεῖσθαι), to which\nhe adheres throughout the passage, is a question which agitated the\nNeoplatonists[1525] somewhat needlessly. The phrase is intended either\nliterally throughout or allegorically throughout. If it be allegorical,\nthe meaning must be that all human souls shall enter again into human\nbodies, but that they shall start this new phase of existence with the\nqualities of lust, violence, respectability, or real virtue and purity,\nacquired in the previous life--merely resembling, as nearly as men may,\nasses, wolves, bees, or gods. Now as regards the first three classes,\nthis allegorical interpretation, if a little forced, is feasible\nenough; but what of the fourth class? Shall the soul which has attained\npurity, the very negation of fleshliness in Plato’s view, suffer\nre-incarnation and struggle once more against the flesh? Surely the\nallegorical explanation is at once condemned. The phrase was intended\nliterally[1526]. Plato signified the re-incarnation of the lustful,\nthe violent, and the merely respectable, in the forms of animals of\nlike character, and he signified--I must not say the re-incarnation,\nfor Plato’s gods were spiritual and not carnal--but the regeneration\nof the pure in the form of gods. And in the same spirit Plutarch too\ncontemplated the possibility of some men’s souls becoming first heroes,\nand from heroes rising to the rank of ‘daemons,’ and from ‘daemons’\ncoming to share, albeit but rarely, in real godhead[1527].\n\nThus even the highest aspirations of the most spiritually-minded of\npagan thinkers owed much to the purely popular religion. The Orphic\ntablet links up the popular conception of death as a wedding with the\nPlatonic conception of the deification of the soul. ‘I was admitted to\nthe embrace of Despoina, Queen of the underworld’: ‘Happy and Blessed\nOne, thou shalt be God instead of mortal.’\n\nBut if Plato, even in his conception of a purely spiritual life\nhereafter, owed something to the popular religion, he drew upon it\nfar more freely in his conception of Love. In the _Symposium_ one\nspeech after another culminates in the assertion of that belief which\nfound its highest expression in the mysteries. ‘So then I say,’ says\nPhaedrus, ‘that Love is the most venerable of the gods, the most\nworthy of honour, the most powerful to grant virtue and blessedness\nunto mankind both in life and after death[1528].’ And in the same tone\ntoo Eryximachus: ‘He it is that wields the mightiest power and is\nthe source for us of all blessedness and of our power to have loving\nfellowship both with one another and with the gods that are stronger\nthan we[1529].’ And finally Aristophanes: It is Love, ‘who in this\npresent life gives us most joys by drawing like unto like, and for our\nhereafter displays hopes most high, if we for our part display piety\ntowards the gods, that he will restore us to our erstwhile nature and\nwill heal us and will make us happy and blessed[1530].’\n\nThis is not Platonic philosophy but popular religion. Phrase after\nphrase reveals the origin of this conception of Love. The hopes most\nhigh were the hopes held forth by the mysteries; the blessedness and\nthe loving fellowship with gods were the fulfilment of those hopes.\nIn such language did men ever hint at the joys to which their mystic\nsacraments gave access. And Plato here ventures yet further. The author\nof those high hopes, the founder of that blessedness, he proclaims, is\nnone other than Love--Love that appealed not to the soul only of the\ninitiated, but to the whole man, both soul and body--Love that meant\nnot only the yearning after wisdom and holiness and spiritual equality\nwith the gods, but that same passion which drew together man and woman,\ngod and goddess--the passion of mankind for their deities, fed in this\nlife by manifold means of communion and even by sacramental union,\nsatisfied hereafter in the full fruition of wedded bliss."
}

  "passage_text": "PREFACE.

Plutarch, who was born at Chaeronea in Boeotia, probably about A.D. 50,
and was a contemporary of Tacitus and Pliny, has written two works still
extant, the well-known _Lives_, and the less-known _Moralia_. The
_Lives_ have often been translated, and have always been a popular work.
Great indeed was their power at the period of the French Revolution. The
_Moralia_, on the other hand, consisting of various Essays on various
subjects (only twenty-six of which are directly ethical, though they
have given their name to the _Moralia_), are declared by Mr. Paley "to
be practically almost unknown to most persons in Britain, even to those
who call themselves scholars."[1] _Habent etiam sua fata libelli._

In older days the _Moralia_ were more valued. Montaigne, who was a great
lover of Plutarch, and who observes in one passage of his Essays that
"Plutarch and Seneca were the only two books of solid learning he
seriously settled himself to read," quotes as much from the _Moralia_ as
from the _Lives_. And in the seventeenth century I cannot but think the
_Moralia_ were largely read at our Universities, at least at the
University of Cambridge. For, not to mention the wonderful way in which
the famous Jeremy Taylor has taken the cream of "Conjugal Precepts" in
his Sermon called "The Marriage Ring," or the large and copious use he
has made in his "Holy Living" of three other Essays in this volume,
namely, those "On Curiosity," "On Restraining Anger," and "On
Contentedness of Mind," proving conclusively what a storehouse he found
the _Moralia_, we have evidence that that most delightful poet, Robert
Herrick, read the _Moralia_, too, when at Cambridge, so that one cannot
but think it was a work read in the University course generally in those
days. For in a letter to his uncle written from Cambridge, asking for
books or money for books, he makes the following remark: "How kind
Arcisilaus the philosopher was unto Apelles the painter, Plutark in his
Morals will tell you."[2]

In 1882 the Reverend C. W. King, Senior Fellow of Trinity College,
Cambridge, translated the six "Theosophical Essays" of the _Moralia_,
forming a volume in Bohn's Classical Library. The present volume
consists of the twenty-six "Ethical Essays," which are, in my opinion,
the cream of the _Moralia_, and constitute a highly interesting series
of treatises on what might be called "The Ethics of the Hearth and
Home." I have grouped these Essays in such a manner as to enable the
reader to read together such as touch on the same or on kindred
subjects.

As is well known, the text of the _Moralia_ is very corrupt, and the
reading very doubtful, in many places. In eight of the twenty-six Essays
in this volume I have had the invaluable help of the text of Rudolf
Hercher; help so invaluable that one cannot but sadly regret that only
one volume of the _Moralia_ has yet appeared in the _Bibliotheca
Teubneriana_. Wyttenbach's text and notes I have always used when
available, and when not so have fallen back upon Reiske. Reiske is
always ingenious, but too fond of correcting a text, and the criticism
of him by Wyttenbach is perhaps substantially correct. "In nullo
auctore habitabat; vagabatur per omnes: nec apud quemquam tamdiu
divertebat, ut in paulo interiorem ejus consuetudinem se insinuaret." I
have also had constantly before me the Didot Edition of the _Moralia_,
edited by Frederic Duebner.

Let any reader who wishes to know more about Plutarch, consult the
article on Plutarch, in the Ninth Edition of the _Encyclopaedia
Britannica_, by the well-known scholar F. A. Paley. He will also do well
to read an Essay on Plutarch by R. W. Emerson, reprinted in Volume III.
of the Bohn's Standard Library Edition of Emerson's Works, and Five
Lectures on Plutarch by the late Archbishop Trench, published by Messrs.
Macmillan and Co. in 1874. All these contain much of interest, and will
repay perusal.

In conclusion, I hope this little volume will be the means of making
popular some of the best thoughts of one of the most interesting and
thoughtful of the ancients, who often seems indeed almost a modern.

To speak generally, what we are wont to say about the arts and\nsciences is also true of moral excellence, for to its perfect\ndevelopment three things must meet together, natural ability, theory,\nand practice. Now the foundation must be laid in training, and practice\ngives facility, but perfection is attained only by the junction of all\nthree. For if any one of these elements be wanting, excellence must be\nso far deficient. For natural ability without training is blind: and\ntraining without natural ability is defective, and practice without both\nnatural ability and training is imperfect. For just as in farming the\nfirst requisite is good soil, next a good farmer, next good seed, so\nalso here: the soil corresponds to natural ability, the training to the\nfarmer, the seed to precepts and instruction. And what trees do not by\nneglect become gnarled and unfruitful, whereas by pruning they become\nfruitful and productive? And what constitution so good but it is marred\nand impaired by sloth, luxury, and too full habit? And what weak\nconstitution has not derived benefit from exercise and athletics? For this supplying them with food is as it\nwere a tightener of love, for even the brute creation, if taken away\nfrom their young, pine away, as we constantly see. Mothers must\ntherefore, as I said, certainly try to suckle their own children: but if\nthey are unable to do so either through physical weakness (for this\ncontingency sometimes occurs), or in haste to have other children, they\nmust select wet and dry nurses with the greatest care, and not introduce\ninto their houses any kind of women. First and foremost they must be\nGreeks in their habits. For just as it is necessary immediately after\nbirth to shapen the limbs of children, so that they may grow straight\nand not crooked, so from the beginning must their habits be carefully\nattended to. For infancy is supple and easily moulded, and what\nchildren learn sinks deeply into their souls while they are young and\ntender, whereas everything hard is softened only with great difficulty.\nFor just as seals are impressed on soft wax, so instruction leaves its\npermanent mark on the minds of those still young. And divine Plato seems\nto me to give excellent advice to nurses not to tell their children any\nkind of fables, that their souls may not in the very dawn of existence\nbe full of folly or corruption.[9] Phocylides the poet also seems to\ngive admirable advice when he says, \"We must teach good habits while the\npupil is still a boy.\"\n\nSec.VI. For as those who are fond of quoting proverbs say not\namiss, \"If you live with a lame man, you will learn to halt.\"[10]"
}

  "passage_text": "Sec.VII. Next, when our boys are old enough to be put into the hands of\ntutors,[11] great care must be taken that we do not hand them over to\nslaves, or foreigners, or flighty persons. For what happens nowadays in\nmany cases is highly ridiculous: good slaves are made farmers, or\nsailors, or merchants, or stewards, or money-lenders; but if they find a\nwinebibbing, greedy, and utterly useless slave, to him parents commit\nthe charge of their sons, whereas the good tutor ought to be such a one\nas was Phoenix, the tutor of Achilles. The point also which I am now\ngoing to speak about is of the utmost importance. The schoolmasters we\nought to select for our boys should be of blameless life, of pure\ncharacter, and of great experience. For a good training is the source\nand root of gentlemanly behaviour. And just as farmers prop up their\ntrees, so good schoolmasters prop up the young by good advice and\nsuggestions, that they may become upright. How one must despise,\ntherefore, some fathers, who, whether from ignorance or inexperience,\nbefore putting the intended teachers to the test, commit their sons to\nthe charge of untried and untested men. If they act so through\ninexperience it is not so ridiculous; but it is to the remotest degree\nabsurd when, though perfectly aware of both the inexperience and\nworthlessness of some schoolmasters, they yet entrust their sons to\nthem; some overcome by flattery, others to gratify friends who solicit\ntheir favours; acting just as if anybody ill in body, passing over the\nexperienced physician, should, to gratify his friend, call him in, and\nso throw away his life; or as if to gratify one's friend one should\nreject the best pilot and choose him instead. Zeus and all the gods! can\nanyone bearing the sacred name of father put obliging a petitioner\nbefore obtaining the best education for his sons? Were they not then\nwise words that the time-honoured Socrates used to utter, and say that\nhe would proclaim, if he could, climbing up to the highest part of the\ncity, \"Men, what can you be thinking of, who move heaven and earth to\nmake money, while you bestow next to no attention on the sons you are\ngoing to leave that money to?\"[12] I would add to this that such fathers\nact very similarly to a person who should be very careful about his shoe\nbut care nothing about his foot. Many persons also are so niggardly\nabout their children, and indifferent to their interests, that for the\nsake of a paltry saving, they prefer worthless teachers for their\nchildren, practising a vile economy at the expense of their children's\nignorance. _Apropos_ of this, Aristippus on one occasion rebuked an\nempty-headed parent neatly and wittily. For being asked how much money a\nparent ought to pay for his son's education, he answered, \"A thousand\ndrachmae.\" And he replying, \"Hercules, what a price! I could buy a slave\nfor as much;\" Aristippus answered, \"You shall have two slaves then, your\nson and the slave you buy.\"[13] And is it not altogether strange that\nyou accustom your son to take his food in his right hand, and chide him\nif he offers his left, whereas you care very little about his hearing\ngood and sound discourses? I will tell you what happens to such\nadmirable fathers, when they have educated and brought up their sons so\nbadly: when the sons grow to man's estate, they disregard a sober and\nwell-ordered life, and rush headlong into disorderly and low vices; then\nat the last the parents are sorry they have neglected their education,\nbemoaning bitterly when it is too late their sons' debasement. For some\nof them keep flatterers and parasites in their retinue--an accursed set\nof wretches, the defilers and pest of youth; others keep mistresses and\ncommon prostitutes, wanton and costly; others waste their money in\neating; others come to grief through dice and revelling; some even go in\nfor bolder profligacy, being whoremongers and defilers of the marriage\nbed,[14] who would madly pursue their darling vice if it cost them their\nlives. Had they associated with some philosopher, they would not have\nlowered themselves by such practices, but would have remembered the\nprecept of Diogenes, whose advice sounds rather low, but is really of\nexcellent moral intent,[15] \"Go into a brothel, my lad, that you may see\nthe little difference between vice and virtue.\""

  "passage_text": "Sec. VIII. I say, then, to speak comprehensively (and I might be justly\nconsidered in so saying to speak as an oracle, not to be delivering a\nmere precept), that a good education and sound bringing-up is of the\nfirst and middle and last importance; and I declare it to be most\ninstrumental and conducive to virtue and happiness. For all other human\nblessings compared to this are petty and insignificant. For noble birth\nis a great honour, but it is an advantage from our forefathers. And\nwealth is valuable, but it is the acquisition of fortune, who has often\ntaken it away from those who had it, and brought it to those who little\nexpected it; and much wealth is a sort of mark for villanous slaves and\ninformers to shoot at to fill their own purses; and, what is a most\nimportant point, even the greatest villains have money sometimes. And\nglory is noble, but insecure. And beauty is highly desirable, but\nshortlived. And health is highly valuable, but soon impaired. And\nstrength is desirable, but illness or age soon made sad inroads into it.\nAnd generally speaking, if anyone prides himself on his bodily strength,\nlet him know that he is deficient in judgment. For how much inferior is\nthe strength of a man to that of animals, as elephants, bulls, and\nlions! But education is of all our advantages the only one immortal and\ndivine. And two of the most powerful agencies in man's nature are mind\nand reason. And mind governs reason, and reason obeys mind; and mind is\nirremovable by fortune, cannot be taken away by informers, cannot be\ndestroyed by disease, cannot have inroads made into it by old age. For\nthe mind alone flourishes in age; and while time takes away everything\nelse, it adds wisdom to old age. Even war, that sweeps away everything\nelse like a winter torrent, cannot take away education. And Stilpo, the\nMegarian, seems to me to have made a memorable answer when Demetrius\nenslaved Megara and rased it to the ground. On his asking whether Stilpo\nhad lost anything, he replied, \"Certainly not, for war can make no havoc\nof virtue.\" Corresponding and consonant to this is the answer of\nSocrates, who when asked, I think by Gorgias,[16] if he had any\nconception as to the happiness of the King of Persia, replied, \"I do not\nknow his position in regard to virtue and education: for happiness lies\nin these, and not in adventitious advantages.\""
}

And as I advise parents to think nothing more important than the\neducation of their children, so I maintain that it must be a sound and\nhealthy education, and that our sons must be kept as far as possible\nfrom vulgar twaddle. For what pleases the vulgar displeases the wise. I\nam borne out by the lines of Euripides, \"Unskilled am I in the oratory\nthat pleases the mob; but amongst the few that are my equals I am\nreckoned rather wise. For those who are little thought of by the wise,\nseem to hit the taste of the vulgar.\"[17] And I have myself noticed\nthat those who practise to speak acceptably and to the gratification of\nthe masses promiscuously, for the most part become also profligate and\nlovers of pleasure in their lives. Naturally enough. For if in giving\npleasure to others they neglect the noble, they would be hardly likely\nto put the lofty and sound above a life of luxury and pleasure, and to\nprefer moderation to delights. Yet what better advice could we give our\nsons than to follow this? or to what could we better exhort them to\naccustom themselves? For perfection is only attained by neither speaking\nnor acting at random--as the proverb says, _Perfection is only attained\nby practice_.[18] Whereas extempore oratory is easy and facile, mere\nwindbag, having neither beginning nor end. It is recorded by tradition that Pericles, when called on\nby the people for a speech, frequently refused on the plea that he was\nunprepared. Similarly Demosthenes, his state-rival, when the Athenians\ncalled upon him for his advice, refused to give it, saying, \"I am not\nprepared.\" But this you will say, perhaps, is mere tradition without\nauthority. But in his speech against Midias he plainly sets forth the\nutility of preparation, for he says, \"I do not deny, men of Athens, that\nI have prepared this speech to the best of my ability: for I should have\nbeen a poor creature if, after suffering so much at his hands, and even\nstill suffering, I had neglected how to plead my case.\"[19] Not that I\nwould altogether reject extempore oratory, or its use in critical cases,\nbut it should be used only as one would take medicine.[20] Up, indeed,\nto man's estate I would have no extempore speaking, but when anyone's\npowers of speech are rooted and grounded, then, as emergencies call for\nit, I would allow his words to flow freely. For as those who have been\nfor a long time in fetters stumble if unloosed, not being able to walk\nfrom being long used to their fetters, so those who for a long time have\nused compression in their words, if they are suddenly called upon to\nspeak off-hand, retain the same character of expression. But to let mere\nlads speak extempore is to give rise to the acme of foolish talk. A\nwretched painter once showed Apelles, they say, a picture, and said, \"I\nhave just done it.\" Apelles replied, \"Without your telling me, I should\nknow it was painted quickly; I only wonder you haven't painted more such\nin the time.\" As then (for I now return from my digression), I advise to\navoid stilted and bombastic language, so again do I urge to avoid a\nfinical and petty style of speech; for tall talk is unpopular, and petty\nlanguage makes no impression. And as the body ought to be not only sound\nbut in good condition, so speech ought to be not only not feeble but\nvigorous. For a safe mediocrity is indeed praised, but a bold\nventuresomeness is also admired. I am also of the same opinion with\nregard to the disposition of the soul, which ought to be neither\naudacious nor timid and easily dejected: for the one ends in impudence\nand the other in servility; but to keep in all things the mean between\nextremes is artistic and proper. And, while I am still on this topic, I\nwish to give my opinion, that I regard a monotonous speech first as no\nsmall proof of want of taste, next as likely to generate disdain, and\ncertain not to please long. For to harp on one string is always tiresome\nand brings satiety; whereas variety is pleasant always whether to the\near or eye."
}

  "passage_text": "Sec. X. Next our freeborn lad ought to go in for a course of what is called
general knowledge, but a smattering of this will be sufficient, a taste
as it were (for perfect knowledge of all subjects would be impossible);
but he must seriously cultivate philosophy. I borrow an illustration to
show my meaning: it is well to sail round many cities, but advantageous
to live in the best. It was a witty remark of the philosopher Bion,[21]
that, as those suitors who could not seduce Penelope took up with her
maids as a _pis aller_, so those who cannot attain philosophy wear
themselves out in useless pursuits. Philosophy, therefore, ought to be
regarded as the most important branch of study. For as regards the cure
of the body, men have found two branches, medicine and exercise: the
former of which gives health, and the latter good condition of body; but
philosophy is the only cure for the maladies and disorders of the soul.
For with her as ruler and guide we can know what is honourable, what is
disgraceful; what is just, what unjust; generally speaking, what is to
be sought after, what to be avoided; how we ought to behave to the gods,
to parents, to elders, to the laws, to foreigners, to rulers, to
friends, to women, to children, to slaves: viz., that we ought to
worship the gods, honour parents, reverence elders, obey the laws,
submit ourselves to rulers, love our friends, be chaste in our relations
with women, kind to our children, and not to treat our slaves badly;
and, what is of the greatest importance, to be neither over elated in
prosperity nor over depressed in adversity,[22] nor to be dissolute in
pleasures, nor fierce and brutish in anger. These I regard as the
principal blessings that philosophy teaches. For to enjoy prosperity
nobly shows a man; and to enjoy it without exciting envy shows a
moderate man; and to conquer the passions by reason argues a wise man;
and it is not everybody who can keep his temper in control. And those
who can unite political ability with philosophy I regard as perfect men,
for I take them to attain two of the greatest blessings, serving the
state in a public capacity, and living the calm and tranquil life of
philosophy. For, as there are three kinds of life, the practical, the
contemplative, and the life of enjoyment, and of these three the one
devoted to enjoyment is a paltry and animal life, and the practical
without philosophy an unlovely and harsh life, and the contemplative
without the practical a useless life, so we must endeavour with all our
power to combine public life with philosophy as far as circumstances
will permit. Such was the life led by Pericles, by Archytas of Tarentum,
by Dion of Syracuse, by Epaminondas the Theban, one of whom was a
disciple of Plato (viz., Dion). And as to education, I do not know that
I need dwell any more on it. But in addition to what I have said, it is
useful, if not necessary, not to neglect to procure old books, and to
make a collection of them, as is usual in agriculture. For the use of
books is an instrument in education, and it is profitable in learning to
go to the fountain head.

Sec. XI. Exercise also ought not to be neglected, but we ought to send our
boys to the master of the gymnasium to train them duly, partly with a
view to carrying the body well, partly with a view to strength. For good
habit of body in boys is the foundation of a good old age. For as in
fine weather we ought to lay up for winter, so in youth one ought to
form good habits and live soberly so as to have a reserve stock of
strength for old age. Yet ought we to husband the exertions of the body,
so as not to be wearied out by them and rendered unfit for study. For,
as Plato says,[23] excessive sleep and fatigue are enemies to learning.
But why dwell on this? For I am in a hurry to pass to the most important
point. Our lads must be trained for warlike encounters, making
themselves efficient in hurling the javelin and darts, and in the chase.
For the possessions of those who are defeated in battle belong to the
conquerors as booty of war; and war is not the place for delicately
brought up bodies: it is the spare warrior that makes the best
combatant, who as an athlete cuts his way through the ranks of the
enemies. Supposing anyone objects: "How so? As you undertook to give
advice on the education of freeborn children, do you now neglect the
poor and plebeian ones, and give instructions only suitable to the
rich?" It is easy enough to meet such critics. I should prefer to make
my teaching general and suitable to all; but if any, through their
poverty, shall be unable to follow up my precepts, let them blame
fortune, and not the author of these hints. We must try with all our
might to procure the best education for the poor as well as the rich,
but if that is impossible, then we must put up with the practicable. I
inserted those matters into my discourse here, that I might hereafter
confine myself to all that appertains to the right education of the
young.

Sec. XII. And this I say that we ought to try to draw our boys to good
pursuits by entreaties and exhortation, but certainly not by blows or
abusive language. For that seems to be more fitting for slaves than the
freeborn. For slaves try to shirk and avoid their work, partly because
of the pain of blows, partly on account of being reviled. But praise or
censure are far more useful than abuse to the freeborn, praise pricking
them on to virtue, censure deterring them from vice. But one must
censure and praise alternately: when they are too saucy we must censure
them and make them ashamed of themselves, and again encourage them by
praise, and imitate those nurses who, when their children sob, give them
the breast to comfort them. But we must not puff them up and make them
conceited with excessive praise, for that will make them vain and give
themselves airs."

While they are in too great a hurry to\nmake their sons take the lead in everything, they lay too much work upon\nthem, so that they faint under their tasks, and, being overburdened, are\ndisinclined for learning. For just as plants grow with moderate rain,\nbut are done for by too much rain, so the mind enlarges by a proper\namount of work, but by too much is unhinged. We must therefore give our\nboys remission from continuous labour, bearing in mind that all our life\nis divided into labour and rest; thus we find not only wakefulness but\nsleep, not only war but peace, not only foul weather but fine also, not\nonly working days but also festivals. And, to speak concisely, rest is\nthe sauce of labour. And we can see this not only in the case of\nanimate, but even inanimate things, for we make bows and lyres slack\nthat we may be able to stretch them. And generally the body is preserved\nby repletion and evacuation, and the soul by rest and work. We ought\nalso to censure some fathers who, after entrusting their sons to tutors\nand preceptors, neither see nor hear how the teaching is done. This is a\ngreat mistake. For they ought after a few days to test the progress of\ntheir sons, and not to base their hopes on the behaviour of a hireling;\nand the preceptors will take all the more pains with the boys, if they\nhave from time to time to give an account of their progress. Hence the\npropriety of that remark of the groom, that nothing fats the horse so\nmuch as the king's eye.[24] And especial attention, in my opinion, must\nbe paid to cultivating and exercising the memory of boys, for memory is,\nas it were, the storehouse of learning; and that was why they fabled\nMnemosyne to be the mother of the Muses, hinting and insinuating that\nnothing so generates and contributes to the growth of learning as\nmemory. And therefore the memory must be cultivated, whether boys have a\ngood one by nature, or a bad one. For we shall so add to natural good\nparts, and make up somewhat for natural deficiencies, so that the\ndeficient will be better than others, and the clever will outstrip\nthemselves. For good is that remark of Hesiod, \"If to a little you keep\nadding a little, and do so frequently, it will soon be a lot.\"[25] And\nlet not fathers forget, that thus cultivating the memory is not only\ngood for education, but is also a great aid in the business of life. For\nthe remembrance of past actions gives a good model how to deal wisely in\nfuture ones.\n\nSec. XIV. We must also keep our sons from filthy language. For, as\nDemocritus says, Language is the shadow of action. They must also be\ntaught to be affable and courteous. For as want of affability is justly\nhateful, so boys will not be disagreeable to those they associate with,\nif they yield occasionally in disputes. For it is not only excellent to\nknow how to conquer, but also to know how to be defeated, when victory\nwould be injurious, for there is such a thing as a Cadmean victory.[26]\nI can cite wise Euripides as a witness of the truth of what I say, who\nsays, \"When two are talking, and one of them is in a passion, he is the\nwiser who first gives way.\"[27]"

That is, that life must be spent without luxury,\nthe tongue must be under control, so must the temper and the hands. All\nthis is of extreme importance, as I will show by examples. To begin with\nthe last case, some who have put their hands to unjust gains, have lost\nall the fruits of their former life, as the Lacedaemonian Gylippus,[28]\nwho was exiled from Sparta for embezzling the public money. To be able\nto govern the temper also argues a wise man. For Socrates, when a very\nimpudent and disgusting young fellow kicked him on one occasion, seeing\nall the rest of his class vexed and impatient, even to the point of\nwanting to prosecute the young man, said, \"What! If a young ass kicked\nme would you have me kick it back?\" Not that the young fellow committed\nthis outrage on Socrates with impunity, for as all reviled him and\nnicknamed him the kicker, he hung himself. And when Aristophanes brought\nhis \"_Clouds_\" on the stage, and bespattered Socrates with his gibes and\nflouts, and one of the spectators said, \"Aren't you vexed, Socrates, at\nhis exhibiting you on the stage in this comic light?\" he answered, \"Not\nI, by Zeus, for I look upon the theatre as only a large supper\nparty.\"[29] Very similar to this was the behaviour of Archytas of\nTarentum and Plato. And that is, I think, the\nreason why the ancients instituted the mysteries that we, learning\ntherein to be silent, might transfer our secrecy to the gods to human\naffairs. And no one ever yet repented of his silence, while multitudes\nhave repented of their speaking. And what has not been said is easy to\nsay, while what has been once said can never be recalled. I have heard\nof myriads who have fallen into the greatest misfortunes through\ninability to govern their tongues. Passing over the rest, I will mention\none or two cases in point. The same Theocritus put\nAntigonus, the King of the Macedonians, a one-eyed man, into a\nthundering rage by alluding to his misfortune. For the King sent his\nchief cook, Eutropio, an important person at his court, to go and fetch\nTheocritus before him to confer with him, and when he had frequently\nrequested him to come without avail, Theocritus at last said, \"I know\nwell you wish to serve me up raw to the Cyclops;\" flouting the King as\none-eyed and the cook with his profession. Eutropio replied, \"You shall\nlose your head, and pay the penalty for this babbling and mad\ninsolence;\" and reported his words to the King, who sent and had his\nhead taken off. Our boys must also be taught to speak the truth as a\nmost sacred duty; for to lie is servile, and most hateful in all men,\nhardly to be pardoned even in poor slaves."
}

  "passage_text": "Sec. XV. Thus much have I said about the good conduct and self-control of\nboys without any doubt or hesitation: but as to what I am now going to\nsay I am doubtful and undecided, and like a person weighed in the scales\nagainst exactly his weight, and feel great hesitation as to whether I\nshould recommend or dissuade the practice. But I must speak out. The\nquestion is this--whether we ought to let the lovers of our boys\nassociate and be with them, or on the contrary, debar them from their\ncompany and scare them off. For when I look at fathers self-opinionated\nsour and austere, who think their sons having lovers a disgrace not to\nbe borne, I am rather afraid of recommending the practice. But when, on\nthe other hand, I think of Socrates, Xenophon, AEschines, Cebes, and all\nthe company of those men who have approved of male loves, and who have\nintroduced their minions to learning, to high positions in the State,\nand to good morals, I change my opinion, and am moved to emulate those\nmen. And Euripides seems to favour these views in the passage, \"But\nthere is among mortals another love, that of the righteous temperate and\npure soul.\"[32] Nor must we omit the remark of Plato, which seems to mix\nseriousness with mirth, that \"those who have distinguished themselves\nought to be permitted to kiss any handsome boy they like.\"[33] Those\nthen that seek only carnal enjoyment must be kept off, but those that\nlove the soul must be encouraged. And while the loves common at Thebes\nand Elis, and the so-called rape at Crete, must be avoided, the loves of\nAthens and Lacedaemon should be emulated.\n\nSec. XVI. As to this matter, therefore, let every parent follow his\ninclination. And now, as I have spoken about the good and decent\nbehaviour of boys, I shall change my subject and speak a little about\nyouths. For I have often censured the introducers of bad habits, who\nhave set over boys tutors and preceptors, but have given to youths full\nliberty, when they ought, on the contrary, to have watched and guarded\nthem more than boys. For who does not know that the offences of boys are\npetty and easily cured, and proceed from the carelessness of tutors or\nwant of obedience to preceptors; but the faults of young men are often\ngrave and serious, as gluttony, and robbing their fathers, and dice, and\nrevellings, and drinking-bouts, and deflowering of maidens, and seducing\nof married women. Such outbreaks ought to be carefully checked and\ncurbed. For that prime of life is prodigal in pleasure, and frisky, and\nneeds a bridle, so that those parents who do not strongly check that\nperiod, are foolishly, if unawares, giving their youths license for\nvice.[34] Sensible parents, therefore, ought during all that period to\nguard and watch and restrain their youths, by precepts, by threats, by\nentreaties, by advice, by promises, by citing examples,[35] on the one\nhand, of those who have come to ruin by being too fond of pleasure, on\nthe other hand, of those who by their self-control have attained to\npraise and good report. For these are, as it were, the two elements of\nvirtue, hope of honour, and fear of punishment; the former inciting to\ngood practices, the latter deterring from bad."
