  "passage_text": "Sec. XVII. We ought, at all hazards, to keep our boys also from association\nwith bad men, for they will catch some of their villany. This was the\nmeaning of Pythagoras' enigmatical precepts, which I shall quote and\nexplain, as they give no slight momentum towards the acquisition of\nvirtue: as, _Do not touch black tails_: that is, do not associate with\nbad men.[36] _Do not go beyond the balance_: that is, we must pay the\ngreatest attention to justice and not go beyond it. _Do not sit on a\nmeasure_: that is, do not be lazy, but earn tomorrow's bread as well as\nto-day's. _Do not give everyone your right hand_: that is, do not be too\nready to strike up a friendship. _Do not wear a tight ring_: that is,\nlet your life be free, do not bind yourself by a chain. _Do not poke the\nfire with a sword_: that is, do not provoke an angry person, but yield\nto such. _Do not eat the heart_: do not wear away the heart by anxiety.\n_Abstain from beans_: that is, do not meddle in state affairs, for the\nvoting for offices was formerly taken by beans. _Do not put your food in\nthe chamber-pot_: that is, do not throw your pearls before swine, for\nwords are the food of the mind, and the villany of men twist them to a\ncorrupt meaning. _When you have come to the end of a journey do not look\nback_: that is, when people are going to die and see that their end is\nnear, they ought to take it easily and not be dejected. But I will\nreturn from my digression. We must keep our boys, as I said, from\nassociation with all bad men, but especially from flatterers. For, as I\nhave often said to parents, and still say, and will constantly affirm,\nthere is no race more pestilential, nor more sure to ruin youths\nswiftly, than the race of flatterers, who destroy both parents and sons\nroot and branch, making the old age of the one and the youth of the\nothers miserable, holding out pleasure as a sure bait. The sons of the\nrich are by their fathers urged to be sober, but by them to be drunk; by\ntheir fathers to be chaste, by them to wax wanton; by their fathers to\nsave, by them to spend; by their fathers to be industrious, by them to\nbe lazy. For they say, \"'Our life's but a span;'[37] we can only live\nonce; why should you heed your father's threats? he's an old twaddler,\nhe has one foot in the grave; we shall soon hoist him up and carry him\noff to burial.\" Some even pimp for them and supply them with prostitutes\nor even married women, and cut huge slices off the father's savings for\nold age, if they don't run off with them altogether. An accursed tribe,\nfeigning friendship, knowing nothing of real freedom, flatterers of the\nrich, despisers of the poor, drawn to young men by a sort of natural\nlogic,[38] showing their teeth and grinning all over when their patrons\nlaugh,[39] misbegotten brats of fortune and bastard elements in life,\nliving according to the nod of the rich, free in their circumstances,\nbut slaves by inclination, when they are not insulted thinking\nthemselves insulted, because they are parasites to no purpose. So, if\nany father cares for the good bringing-up of his sons, he must banish\nfrom his house this abominable race. He must also be on his guard\nagainst the viciousness of his sons' schoolfellows, for they are quite\nsufficient to corrupt the best morals.\n\nSec. XVIII. What I have said hitherto is _apropos_ to my subject: I will\nnow speak a word to the men. Parents must not be over harsh and rough in\ntheir natures, but must often forgive their sons' offences, remembering\nthat they themselves were once young. And just as doctors by infusing a\nsweet flavour into their bitter potions find delight a passage to\nbenefit, so fathers must temper the severity of their censure by\nmildness; and sometimes relax and slacken the reins of their sons'\ndesires, and again tighten them; and must be especially easy in respect\nto their faults, or if they are angry must soon cool down. For it is\nbetter for a father to be hot-tempered than sullen, for to continue\nhostile and irreconcilable looks like hating one's son. And it is good\nto seem not to notice some faults, but to extend to them the weak sight\nand deafness of old age, so as seeing not to see, and hearing not to\nhear, their doings. We tolerate the faults of our friends; why should we\nnot that of our sons? often even our slaves' drunken debauches we do not\nexpose. Have you been rather near? spend more freely. Have you been\nvexed? let the matter pass. Has your son deceived you by the help of a\nslave? do not be angry. Did he take a yoke of oxen from the field, did\nhe come home smelling of yesterday's debauch? wink at it. Is he scented\nlike a perfume shop? say nothing. Thus frisky youth gets broken in.[40]\n\nSec. XIX. Those of our sons who are given to pleasure and pay little heed\nto rebuke, we must endeavour to marry, for marriage is the surest\nrestraint upon youth. And we must marry our sons to wives not much\nricher or better born, for the proverb is a sound one, \"Marry in your\nown walk of life.\"[41] For those who marry wives superior to themselves\nin rank are not so much the husbands of their wives as unawares slaves\nto their dowries.[42]"
}

away from bad deeds and words. For those fathers who censure their
sons' faults while they themselves commit the same, are really their own

teach our sons self-control, emulating the conduct of Eurydice, who,

herself though late in life, and her love to them is well depicted in
the inscription which she offered to the Muses: "Eurydice of Hierapolis

knowledge. For when a mother with sons full-grown she learnt letters,
the preservers of knowledge."

care, is a thing possible to human nature.[43]

  "passage_text": "Sec. IV. Refer the question to the ancient inhabitants of the earth, to the
first mothers and fathers. There was no law ordering them to have
families, no expectation of advantage or return to be got out of them. I
should rather say that mothers would be likely to be hostile and bear
malice to their babes, owing to the great danger and pains of travail.
And women say the lines, "When the sharp pangs of travail seize on the
pregnant woman, then come to her aid the Ilithyiae, who help women in
hard childbirth, those daughters of Hera, goddesses of travail,"[55]
were not written by Homer, but by some Homerid who had been a mother, or
was even then in the throes of travail, and who vividly felt the sharp
pain in her womb. But the love to one's offspring implanted by nature,
moves and influences the mother even then: in the very height of her
throes, she neglects not nor flees from her babe, but turns to it and
smiles at it, and takes it up and caresses it, though she derives no
pleasure or utility from it, but with pain and sorrow receives it,
"warming it and fostering it in swaddling clothes, with unintermittent
assiduity both night and day."[56] What hope of gain or advantage had
they in those days? nay, or even now? for the hopes of parents are
uncertain, and have to be long waited for. He who plants a vine in the
spring equinox, gleans its vintage in the autumnal equinox; he who sows
corn when the Pleiads set, reaps it when they rise; cattle and horses
and birds have produce at once fit for use; whereas man's bringing up is
toilsome, his growth slow; and as excellence flowers late, most fathers
die before their sons attain to fame. Neocles lived not to see
Themistocles' victory at Salamis, nor Miltiades Cimon's at the
Eurymedon, nor did Xanthippus hear Pericles haranguing, nor did Aristo
hear Plato philosophizing, nor did their fathers know of the triumphs of
Euripides and Sophocles. They heard them faltering in speech and lisping
in syllables, the poor parents saw their errors in revelling and
drinking and love-affairs, so that of all Evenus'[57] lines, that one
alone is most remembered and quoted, "to a father a son is always a
cause of fear or pain." Nevertheless, parents do not cease to bring up
sons, even when they can least need them. For it is ridiculous to
suppose that the rich, when they have sons, sacrifice and rejoice that
they will have people to take care of them and to bury them; unless
indeed they bring up sons from want of heirs; as if one could not find
or fall in with anyone who would be willing to have another's property!
Why, the sand on the sea shore, and the dust, and the wings of birds of
varied note, are less numerous than the number of would-be heirs. For
had Danaus, the father of fifty daughters, been childless, he would have
had more heirs, and of a different spirit. For sons have no gratitude,
nor regard, nor veneration for inheritance; but take it as a debt;
whereas the voices of strangers which you hear round the childless man,
are like those lines in the play, "O People, first bathe, after one
decision in the courts, then eat, drink, gobble, take the
three-obol-piece."[58] And what Euripides has said, "Money finds friends
for men, and has the greatest power among mankind," is not merely a
general truth, but is especially true in the case of the childless. For
those the rich entertain to dinner, those great men pay court to, to
those alone orators give their services gratis. "A mighty personage is a
rich man, whose heir is unknown." It has at any rate made many much
loved and honoured, whom the possession of one child would have made
unloved and insignificant. Whence we see that there is no power or
advantage to be got from children, but that the love of them, alike in
mankind as among the animals, proceeds entirely from nature.

Sec. V. What if this natural affection, like many other virtues, is
obscured by badness, as a wilderness chokes a garden? Are we to say that
man does not love himself by nature, because many cut their throats or
throw themselves down precipices? Did not Oedipus put out his eyes? And
did not Hegesias by his speeches make, many of his hearers to commit
suicide?[59] "Fatality has many different aspects."[60] But all these
are diseases and maladies of the soul driving a man contrary to nature
out of his wits: as men themselves testify even against themselves. For
if a sow destroys one of its litter, or a bitch one of its pups, men are
dejected and troubled, and think it an evil omen, and sacrifice to the
gods to avert any bad results, on the score that it is natural to all to
love and cherish their offspring, unnatural to destroy it. For just as
in mines the gold is conspicuous even though mixed up with earth, so
nature manifests plainly love to offspring even in instances of faulty
habits and affections. For when the poor do not rear their children, it
is from fear that if reared to man's estate they would be more than
ought to be the case servile, and have little culture, and be debarred
of all advantages: so, thinking poverty the worst of all evils, they
cannot bear to give it their children, any more than they would some bad
disease.[61]

    privileges to the father of three children, under the
    Roman Emperors. Frequent allusions are made to this law
    by the ancient writers.

    [46] Compare Lucretius, i. 10-20.

    [47] A quotation from Simonides.

    [48] We are not bound to swallow all the ancients tell
    us. Credat Judaeus Apella!

    [49] "Iliad," xvii. 134-136.

    [50] "Iliad," ix. 324. Quoted again in "How one may be
    aware of one's Progress in Virtue," Sec. 8.

    [51] "Odyssey," xx. 14, 15."
}

FLAVIANUS AND AUTOBULUS, THE OPENERS OF THE DIALOGUE,
ARE BROTHERS. THE OTHER SPEAKERS ARE THEIR FATHER,
DAPHNAEUS, PROTOGENES, PISIAS, AND OTHERS.

I. _Flavianus._--You say that it was on Mount Helicon, Autobulus, that
those conversations took place about Love, which you are now about to
narrate to us at our request, as you either wrote them down, or at least
remember them from frequently asking our father about them.

_Autobulus._--It was on Mount Helicon among the Muses, Flavianus, when
the people of Thespiae were celebrating their Festival to the God of
Love, which they celebrate very magnificently and splendidly every five
years to that God, as also to the Muses.

_Flavianus._--Do you know what all of us who have come to this audience
intend to ask of you?

_Autobulus._--No, but I shall know if you tell me.

_Flavianus._--Remove from your discourse for this once the poet's
meadows and shades, and talk about ivy and yews, and all other
commonplaces of that kind that writers love to introduce, with more zeal
than discretion, in imitation of Plato's Ilissus and the famous willow
and the gentle slope of grass.[62]

_Autobulus._--My dear Flavianus, my narrative needs not any such
exordium. The occasion that caused the conversation simply demands a
chorus for the action and a stage, nothing else is wanting to the drama,
let us only pray to the Mother of the Muses to be propitious, and give
me memory for my narrative.

Sec. II. Long ago our father, before we were born, having lately married
our mother, had gone to sacrifice to the God of Love, in consequence of
a dispute and variance that broke out among their parents, and took our
mother to the Festival, for she also had her part in the vow and
sacrifice. Some of their intimate friends journeyed with them from the
town where they lived, and when they got to Thespiae they found there
Daphnaeus the son of Archidamus, a lover of Lysandra the daughter of
Simo, and of all her suitors the one who stood highest in her favour,
and Soclarus the son of Aristio, who had come from Tithorea. And there
were there also Protogenes of Tarsus, and Zeuxippus from Sparta,
strangers, and my father said most of the most notable Boeotians were
there also. For two or three days they went about the town in one
another's company, as it was likely they would do, quietly carrying on
philosophical discussions in the wrestling-schools and theatres: after
that, to avoid a wearisome contest of harpers, decided beforehand by
canvassing and cabal, most broke up their camp as if they had been in a
hostile country, and removed to Mount Helicon, and bivouacked there with
the Muses. In the morning they were visited by Anthemion and Pisias,
both men of good repute, and very great friends of Baccho, who was
surnamed the Handsome, and also rivals of one another somewhat through
their affection for him. Now you must know that there was at Thespiae a
lady called Ismenodora, famous for her wealth and good family, and of
uncommon good repute for her virtuous life: for she had been a widow
some time without a breath of slander lighting upon her, though she was
young and good-looking. As Baccho was the son of a friend and crony of
hers, she had tried to bring about a marriage between him and a maiden
who was her own relation, but by frequently being in his company and
talking to him she had got rather smitten with him herself. And hearing
much in his favour, and often talking about him, and seeing that many
noble young men were in love with him, she fell violently in love with
him, and, being resolved to do nothing unbecoming to her fair fame,
determined to marry and live openly with him. And the matter seeming in
itself rather odd, Baccho's mother looked rather askance at the proposed
matrimonial alliance as being too high and splendid for her son, while
some of his companions who used to go out hunting with him, frightening
him and flouting him with Ismenodora's being rather too old for him,
really did more to break off the match than those who seriously opposed
it. And Baccho, being only a youth, somehow felt a little ashamed at the
idea of marrying a widow, but, neglecting the opinions of everybody
else, he submitted the decision as to the expediency of the marriage to
Pisias and Anthemion, the latter being his cousin, though older than
him, and the former the gravest[63] of his lovers. Pisias objected to
the marriage, and upbraided Anthemion with throwing the youth away on
Ismenodora. Anthemion replied that it was not well in Pisias, being a
good fellow in other respects, to imitate depraved lovers by shutting
out his friend from house and marriage and wealth, merely that he might
enjoy the sight of him as long as possible naked and in all his virgin
bloom at the wrestling-schools.

Sec. III. To avoid getting estranged by provoking one another on the
question, they came and chose our father and his companions as umpires
on the matter. And of the other friends, as if by concerted arrangement,
Daphnaeus espoused the view of Anthemion, and Protogenes the view of
Pisias. And Protogenes inveighing somewhat too freely against
Ismenodora, Daphnaeus took him up and said, "Hercules, what are we not to
expect, if Protogenes is going to be hostile to love? he whose whole
life, whether in work or at play, has been devoted to love, in
forgetfulness of letters, in forgetfulness of his country, not like
Laius, away from his country only five days, his was only a torpid and
land love: whereas your love 'unfolding its swift wings,' flew over the
sea from Cilicia to Athens, merely to gaze at and saunter about with
handsome boys. For that was the original reason, doubtless, of
Protogenes' journey abroad.""

And some laughter ensuing, Protogenes replied, \"Do I really seem\nto you now to be hostile to love, and not to be fighting for love\nagainst ungovernable lust, which with most disgraceful acts and emotions\nassumes the most honourable of titles?\" Whereupon Daphnaeus, \"Do you call\nthe marriage and union of man and woman most disgraceful, than which no\nholier tie exists nor ever did?\" Protogenes replied, \"Why, as all this\nis necessary for the human race to continue, our legislators do not act\namiss in crying up marriage and eulogizing it to the masses, but of\ngenuine love there is not a particle in the woman's side of a house;[64]\nand I also say that you who are sweet on women and girls only love them\nas flies love milk, and bees the honey-comb, and butchers and cooks\ncalves and birds, fattening them up in darkness.[65] But as nature leads\none to eat and drink moderately and sufficiently, and excess in this is\ncalled gluttony and gormandizing, so the mutual desires between men and\nwomen are natural; but that headlong, violent, and uncontrollable\npassion for the sex is not rightly called love. For love, when it seizes\na noble and young soul, ends in virtue through friendship; but these\nviolent passions for women, at the best, aim only at carnal enjoyment\nand reaping the harvest of a beauteous prime, as Aristippus showed in\nhis answer to one who told him Lais loved him not, 'No more,' he said,\n'do meat and wine love me, but I gladly enjoy both.'[66] For the end of\npassion is pleasure and fruition: but love, when it has once lost the\npromise of friendship, will not remain and continue to cherish merely\nfor beauty that which gives it pain, where it gives no return of\nfriendship and virtue. You remember the husband in the play saying to\nhis wife, 'Do you hate me? I can bear that hatred very easily, since of\nmy dishonour I make money.' Not a whit more really in love than this\nhusband is the one, who, not for gain but merely for the sexual\nappetite, puts up with a peevish and unsympathetic wife, as Philippides,\nthe comic poet, ridiculed the orator, Stratocles, 'You scarce can kiss\nher if she turns her back on you.' If, however, we ought to give the\nname of love to this passion, then is it an effeminate and bastard love,\nand like at Cynosarges,[67] taking us to the woman's side of the house:\nor rather as they say there is a genuine mountain eagle, which Homer\ncalled 'black, and a bird of prey,' and there are other kinds of\nspurious eagles, which catch fish and lazy birds in marshes, and often\nin want of food emit an hungry wail: so the genuine love is the love of\nboys, a love not 'flashing with desire,' as Anacreon said the love of\nmaidens was, nor 'redolent of ointment and sprightly,' but you will see\nit plain and without airs in the schools of the philosophers, or perhaps\nin the gymnasiums and wrestling-schools, keenly and nobly pursuing\nyouths, and urging on to virtue those who are well worthy of attention:\nbut that soft and stay-at-home love, spending all its time in women's\nbosoms and beds, always pursuing effeminate delights, and enervated by\nunmanly, unfriendly, and unimpassioned pleasures, we ought to condemn as\nSolon condemned it: for he forbade slaves to love boys or to anoint them\nwith oil, while he allowed them to associate with women. For friendship\nis noble and refined, whereas pleasure is vulgar and illiberal.\nTherefore, for a slave to love boys is neither liberal or refined: for\nit is merely the love of copulation, as the love of women.\""
}

  "passage_text": "Sec. V. Protogenes was intending to go on at greater length, when Daphnaeus
stopped him and said, "You do well, by Zeus, to mention Solon, and we
too may use him as the test of an amorous man. Does he not define such a
one in the lines, 'As long as you love boys in the glorious flower of
their youth for their kisses and embraces.' And add to Solon the lines
of AEschylus, 'You did not disdain the honour of the thighs, O thankless
one after all my frequent kisses.'[68] For some laugh at them if they
bid lovers, like sacrificing priests and seers, to inspect thighs and
loins; but I think this a mighty argument in behalf of the love of
women. For if the unnatural commerce with males does not take away or
mar the amorous propensity, much more likely is it that the natural love
of women will end in friendship after the favour. For, Protogenes, the
yielding of the female to the male was called by the ancients the
favour. Thus Pindar says Hephaestus was the son of Hera 'without any
favours':[69] and Sappho, addressing a girl not yet ripe for marriage,
says to her, 'You seemed to me a little girl, too young for the favour.'
And someone asks Hercules, 'Did you obtain the girl's favour by force or
by persuasion?' But the love of males for males, whether rape or
voluntary--pathicks effeminately submitting, to use Plato's words, 'to
be treated bestially'--is altogether a foul and unlovely favour. And so
I think Solon wrote the lines quoted above 'in his hot youth,' as Plato
puts it; but when he became older wrote these other lines, 'Now I
delight in Cyprus-born Aphrodite, and in Dionysus, and in the Muses: all
these give joys to men': as if, after the heat and tempest of his boyish
loves, he had got into a quiet haven of marriage and philosophy. But
indeed, Protogenes, if we look at the real facts of the case, the love
for boys and women is really one and the same passion: but if you wish
in a disputatious spirit to make any distinction, you will find that
this boy-love goes beyond all bounds, and, like some late-born and
ill-begotten bastard brat, seeks to expel its legitimate brother the
older love, the love of women. For indeed, friend, it is only yesterday
or the day before, since the strippings and exposures of the youths in
the gymnasiums, that this boy-love crept in, and gently insinuated
itself and got a footing, and at last in a little time got fully-fledged
in the wrestling-schools, and has now got fairly unbearable, and insults
and tramples on conjugal love, that love that gives immortality to our
mortal race, when our nature has been extinguished by death, kindling it
again by new births. And this boy-love denies that pleasure is its aim:
for it is ashamed and afraid to confess the truth: but it needs some
specious excuse for the liberties it takes with handsome boys in their
prime: the pretext is friendship and virtue. So your boy-lover wallows
in the dust, bathes in cold water, raises his eyebrows, gives himself
out for a philosopher, and lives chaste abroad because of the law: but
in the stillness of night

  'Sweet is the ripe fruit when the guard's withdrawn.'[70]

But if, as Protogenes says, there is no carnal intercourse in these
boy-familiarities, how is it Love, if Aphrodite is not present, whom it
is the destiny of Love to cherish and pay court to, and to partake of
just as much honour and power as she assigns to him? But if there is any
Love without Aphrodite, as there is drunkenness without wine in drinks
made from figs and barley, the disturbing it will be fruitless and
without effect, and surfeiting and disgusting."

Sec. VI. At the conclusion of this speech, it was clear that Pisias was
vexed and indignant with Daphnaeus; and after a moment's silence he
began: "O Hercules! what levity and audacity for men to state that they
are tied to women as dogs to bitches, and to banish the god of Love from
the gymnasiums and public walks, and light of day and open intercourse,
and to restrict him to brothels[71] and philtres and incantations of
wanton women: for to chaste women, I am sure, it belongs not either to
love or be loved." At this point our father told me he interposed, and
took Protogenes by the hand, and said to him:

  "'This word of yours rouses the Argive host,'

and of a verity Pisias makes us to side with Daphnaeus by his extravagant
language, charging marriage with being a loveless intercourse, and one
that has no participation in divine friendship, although we can see that
it is an intercourse, if erotic persuasion and favour fail, that cannot
be restrained by shame and fear as by bit and bridle." Thereupon Pisias
said, "I care little about his arguments; but I see that Daphnaeus is in
the same condition as brass: for, just as it is not worked upon so much
by the agency of fire as by the molten and liquid brass fused with it,
so is he not so much captivated by the beauty of Lysandra as by his
association with one who is the victim of the gentle passion; and it is
plain that, if he doesn't take refuge with us, he will soon melt away
in the flame altogether. But I see, what Anthemion would very much like,
that I am offending the Court, so I stop." "You amuse us," said
Anthemion: "but you ought from the first to have spoken to the point.""
}

VII. \"I say then,\" continued Pisias, \"and give it out boldly, as far\nas I am concerned, let every woman have a lover; but we ought to guard\nagainst giving the wealth of Ismenodora to Baccho, lest, if we involve\nhim in so much grandeur and magnificence, we unwittingly lose him in it,\nas tin is lost in brass. And\ntherefore men of sense prune the excessive wealth of their wives, as if\nit had wings that required clipping; for this same wealth implants in\nthem luxury, caprice, and vanity, by which they are often elated and fly\naway altogether: but if they remain, it would be better to be bound by\ngolden fetters, as in Ethiopia, than to a woman's wealth.\"\n\nSec. VIII. Here Protogenes put in, \"You say nothing about the risk we run\nof unseasonably and ridiculously reversing the well-known advice of\nHesiod:\n\n  'If seasonable marriage you would make,\n   Let about thirty be the bridegroom's age,\n   The bride be in the fifth year of her womanhood:'[72]\n\nif we thus marry a lad hardly old enough for marriage to a woman so many\nyears older, than himself, as dates and figs are forced. You will say\nshe loves him passionately: who prevents her, then, from serenading at\nhis doors, singing her amorous ditty, putting garlands on his statues,\nand wrestling and boxing with her rivals in his affections? For all\nthese are what people in love do. And let her lower her eyebrows, and\ngive up the airs of a coquette, and assume the appearance of those that\nare deeply smitten. But if she is modest and chaste, let her decorously\nstay at home and await there her lovers and sweethearts; for any\nsensible man would be disgusted and flee from a woman who took the\ninitiative in love, far less would he be likely to marry her after such\na barefaced wooing.\""

When Protogenes had done speaking, my father said, \"Do you see,\nAnthemion, that they force us to intervene again, who have no objection\nto dance in the retinue of conjugal Love?\" \"I do,\" said Anthemion, \"but\npray defend Love at some length, as you are on his side, and moreover\ncome to the rescue of wealth,[73] with which Pisias seeks to scare us.\"\nThereupon my father began, \"What on earth will not be brought as a\ncharge against a woman, if we are to reject Ismenodora because she is in\nlove and has money? Granted she loves sway and is rich? What then, if\nshe is young and handsome? And what if she plumes herself somewhat on\nthe lustre of her race? Have not chaste women often something of the\nmorose and peevish in their character almost past bearing? Do they not\nsometimes get called waspish and shrewish by virtue of their very\nchastity? Would it be best then to marry off the street some Thracian\nAbrotonus, or some Milesian Bacchis, and seal the bargain by the present\nof a handful of nuts? But we have known even such turn out intolerable\ntyrants, Syrian flute-girls and ballet-dancers, as Aristonica, and\nOenanthe with her tambourine, and Agathoclea, who have lorded it over\nkings' diadems.[74] Why Syrian Semiramis was only the servant and\nconcubine of one of king Ninus's slaves, till Ninus the great king\nseeing and falling in love with her, she got such power over him that\nshe thought so cheap of him, that she asked to be allowed one day to sit\non the royal throne, with the royal diadem on her head, and to transact\nstate affairs. And Ninus having granted her permission, and having\nordered all his subjects to obey her as himself, she first gave several\nvery moderate orders to make trial of the guards; but when she saw that\nthey obeyed her without the slightest hesitation, she ordered them to\nseize Ninus and put him in fetters, and at last put him to death; and\nall her commands being obeyed, she ruled over Asia for a long time with\ngreat lustre. And was not Belestiche a foreign woman off the streets,\nalthough at Alexandria she has shrines and temples, with an inscription\nas Aphrodite Belestiche, which she owes to the king's love? And she who\nhas in this very town[75] a temple and rites in common with Eros, and at\nDelphi stands in gold among kings and queens, by what dowry got she her\nlovers? But just as the lovers of Semiramis, Belestiche, and Phryne,\nbecame their prey unconsciously through their weakness and effeminacy,\nso on the other hand poor and obscure men, having contracted alliances\nwith rich women of rank, have not been thereby spoilt nor merged their\npersonality, but have lived with their wives on a footing of kindness,\nyet still kept their position as heads of the house. But he that abases\nhis wife and makes her small, like one who tightens the ring on a finger\ntoo small for it fearing it will come off,[76] is like those who cut\ntheir mares' tails off and then take them to a river or pond to drink,\nwhen they say that sorrowfully discerning their loss of beauty these\nmares lose their self-respect and allow themselves to be covered by\nasses.[77] To select a wife for wealth rather than for her excellence or\nfamily is dishonourable and illiberal; but it is silly to reject wealth\nwhen it is accompanied by excellence and family. Antigonus indeed wrote\nto his officer who had garrisoned Munychia[78] to make not only the\ncollar strong but the dog lean, that he might undermine the strength of\nthe Athenians; but it becomes not the husband of a rich or handsome\nwoman to make his wife poor or ugly, but by his self-control and good\nsense, and by not too extravagantly showing his admiration for her, to\nexhibit himself as her equal not her slave, and (to borrow an\nillustration from the scales) to add just so much weight to his\ncharacter as shall over-balance her, yet only just. Moreover, both\nIsmenodora and Baccho are of a suitable age for marriage and procreation\nof children; Ismenodora, I hear, is still in her prime, and\" (here my\nfather smiled slily at Pisias) \"she is certainly not a bit older than\nher rivals, and has no grey hairs, as some of those who consort with\nBaccho have. And if their union is seasonable, who knows but that she\nmay be a better partner for him than any young woman? For young couples\ndo not blend and mix well together, and it takes a long time and is not\nan easy process for them to divest themselves of their pride and spirit,\nand at first there's a good deal of dirty weather and they don't pull\nwell together, and this is oftenest the case when there's love on both\nsides, and, just as a storm wrecks the ship if no pilot is on board, so\ntheir marriage is trouble and confusion, neither party knowing how\neither to rule or to give way properly. And if the baby is under the\nnurse, and the boy under the master, and the lad under the master of the\ngymnasium, and the youth under his lover, and the full-grown man under\nthe law and magistrate, and no one is his own master and exempt from\nobedience to someone, what wonder would it be if a sensible woman rather\nolder than her husband would direct well the life of a young man, being\nuseful to him by reason of her superior wisdom, and acceptable to him\nfor her sweetness and gentleness? And to sum up the whole matter,\" said\nhe, \"we Boeotians ought to revere Hercules, and so find no fault in any\ninequality of age in marriages, seeing that he gave his own wife Megara\nin marriage to Iolaus, though he was only sixteen and she\nthree-and-thirty.\"[79]"
}

Pisias came galloping up from the town to report an act of marvellous
audacity. Ismenodora, it appears, thinking Baccho had no personal
dislike to the match, but only stood in awe of his friends who tried to
dissuade him from it, determined that she would not let the young fellow
slip through her fingers. Accordingly, she sent for the most active and
intimate[80] of her male friends, and for some of her female cronies,
and instructed them as to what part they should play, and waited for the
hour when Baccho was accustomed regularly to pass by her house on his
way to the wrestling-school. And as he passed by on this occasion with
two or three of his companions, anointed for the exercise, Ismenodora
met him at the door and just touched his cloak, and her friends rushed
out all together and prettily seized the pretty fellow as he was in his
cloak and jersey,[81] and hurried him into the house and at once locked
the doors. And the women inside at once divested him of his cloak and
put on him a bridal robe; and the servants ran about the town and put
olive wreaths and laurel garlands at the doors of Baccho's house as well
as Ismenodora's, and a flute-girl went up and down the street playing
and singing the wedding-song. And some of the inhabitants of Thespiae and
the strangers laughed, others were indignant and tried to make the
superintendents of the gymnasium move in the matter, for they have great
power in Thespiae over the youths, and pay great attention to their
actions. And now there was no more talk about the sports, but everyone
left the theatre for the neighbourhood of Ismenodora's house, and there
stood in groups talking and disputing about what had happened.

Sec. XI. Now when Pisias' friend had come up like an _aide-de-camp_ in war,
"bloody with spurring, fiery red with haste," to report this news that
Ismenodora had seized Baccho, my father said that Zeuxippus smiled, and
being a great lover of Euripides repeated the line,

  "Lady, though rich, thou hast thy sex's feelings."

But Pisias jumped up and cried out, "Ye gods, what will be the end of
license like this which will overthrow our town? Already we are fast
tending to lawlessness through our independence. And yet it is perhaps
ridiculous to be indignant about law and justice, when nature itself is
trampled upon by being thus subjected to women? Saw even Lemnos ever the
like of this?[82] Let us go," he continued, "let us go and hand over to
the women the gymnasium and council-hall, if the townsmen have lost all
their nerve." Pisias then left the company, and Protogenes went with
him, partly sympathizing with his indignation, but still endeavouring to
cool him. And Anthemion said, "'Twas a bold deed and certainly does
savour somewhat of Lemnos--I own it now we are alone--this Ismenodora
must be most violently in love." Hereupon Soclarus said, with a sly
smile, "You don't think then that this rape and detention was an excuse
and stratagem on the part of a wily young man to escape from the
clutches of his lovers, and fly of his own volition to the arms of a
rich and handsome widow?" "Pray don't say so, Soclarus," said Anthemion,
"pray don't entertain any such suspicions of Baccho, for even if he were
not by nature most simple and naive, he would not have concealed the
matter from me to whom he divulges all his secrets, especially as he
knows that I have always been very anxious he should marry Ismenodora.
But as Heraclitus says truly, It is more difficult to control love than
anger; for whatever love has a fancy to, it will buy even at the cost of
life, money, and reputation. Who lives a more quiet life in our town
than Ismenodora? When did ever any ugly rumour attach itself to her?
When did ever any breath of suspicion sully her house? Some divine
inspiration, beyond human calculation, seems now to have possessed her."

Sec. XII. Then Pemptides laughed and said, "Of course you know that there
is a certain disease of the body called the sacred disease.[83] It is no
wonder, therefore, if some call the greatest and most insane passion of
the soul sacred and divine. However, as in Egypt I once saw two
neighbours disputing when a serpent passed by them on the road, both
calling it a good omen, but each claiming the blessing as his alone; so
seeing lately that some of you drag Love to the men's apartments, while
others confine it to the women's side of the house, while all of you
regard it as a divine and superlative blessing, I do not wonder, since
it is a passion that has such power and honour, that those who ought to
banish it from every quarter and clip its wings do themselves add to its
influence and power. And hitherto I held my peace, for I saw that the
discussion turned rather on private than public interests, but now that
we have got rid of Pisias, I would gladly hear from you to what they had
an eye who first called Love a god."

answer his question, another messenger came from the town, sent by
Ismenodora to summon Anthemion, for the tumult had increased, and there
was a difference of opinion between the superintendents of the
gymnasium, one thinking they ought to demand the liberation of Baccho,
the other thinking they ought not to interfere. Anthemion got up at once
and went off. And our father, addressing Pemptides especially, said,
"You seem to me, my dear Pemptides, to be handling a great and bold
matter, or rather to be discussing things that ought not to be
discussed, in asking for a reason in each case for our opinion about the
gods. Our ancient and hereditary faith is sufficient, a better argument
than which we cannot either utter or find,

  'Not e'en if wisdom in our brains resides;'[84]"

  "passage_text": "but if this common foundation and basis of all piety be disturbed, and
its stability and time-honoured ideas be unsettled, it becomes
undermined and is suspected by everybody. You have heard, of course,
what hot water Euripides got into, when he wrote at the beginning of his
'Melanippe,'

  'Zeus, whosoe'er he is, I do not know
   Except by hearsay,'[85]

but if he changed the opening line, he had confidence, it seems, that
his play would go down with the public uncommonly well,[86] so he
altered it into

  'Zeus the divine, as he is truly called.'[87]

And what difference is there between calling in question the received
opinion about Zeus or Athene, and that about Love? For it is not now for
the first time that Love asks for an altar and sacrifices, nor is he a
strange god introduced by foreign superstition, as some Attis or Adonis,
furtively smuggled in by hermaphrodites and women, and secretly
receiving honours not his own, to avoid an indictment among the gods for
coming among them under false pretences. And when, my friend, you hear
the words of Empedocles,

  'Friendship is there too, of same length and breadth,
   But with the mind's eye only can you see it,
   Till with the sight your very soul is thralled,'

you must suppose that they refer to Love. For this god is invisible, but
to be extolled by us as one of the very oldest gods. And if you demand
proofs about every one of the gods, laying a profane hand on every
temple, and bringing a learned doubt to every altar, you will scrutinize
and pry into everything. But we need not go far to find Love's pedigree.

  'See you how great a goddess Aphrodite is?
   She 'tis that gave us and engendered Love,
   Whereof come all that on the earth do live.'[88]

And so Empedocles calls Aphrodite _Life-giving_,[89] and Sophocles calls
her _Fruitful_, both very appropriate epithets. And though the wonderful
act of generation belongs to Aphrodite only, and Love is only present in
it as a subordinate, yet if he be absent the whole affair becomes
undesirable, and low, and tame. For a loveless coition brings only
satiety, as the satisfaction of hunger and thirst, and has nothing noble
resulting from it, whereas by Love Aphrodite removes the cloying element
in pleasure, and produces harmonious friendship. And so Parmenides
declares Love to be the oldest of the creations of Aphrodite, writing in
his Cosmogony,

  'Of all the gods first Love she did contrive.'

But Hesiod, more naturally in my opinion, makes Love the most ancient of
all, so that all things derive their existence from him.[90] If we then
deprive Love of his ancient honours, those of Aphrodite will be lost
also. For we cannot argue that, while some revile Love, all spare
Aphrodite, for on the same stage we hear of Love,

  'Love is an idle thing and for the idle:'[91]

and again of Aphrodite,

  'Cypris, my boys, is not her only name,
   For many names has she. She is a hell,
   A power remorseless, nay a raging madness.'[92]

Just as in the case of the other gods there is hardly one that has not
been reviled, or escaped the scurrility of ignorance. Look, for example,
at Ares, who may be considered as it were the counterpart of Love, what
honours he has received from men, and again what abuse, as

  'Ares is blind, ye women, has no eyes,
   And with his pig's snout roots up all good things.'[93]

And Homer calls him 'blood-stained' and 'fickle.'[94] And Chrysippus
brings a grievous charge against him, in defining his name to mean
destroyer,[95] thereby giving a handle to those who think that Ares is
only the fighting, wrangling, and quarrelsome instinct among mankind.
Others again will tell us that Aphrodite is simply desire, and Hermes
eloquence, and the Muses the arts and sciences, and Athene wisdom. You
see what an abyss of impiety opens up before us, if we describe each of
the gods, as only a passion, a power, or a virtue!"

Sec. XIV. "I see it," said Pemptides, "and it is impious either to make the
gods passions, or to do just the contrary, and make the passions gods."
"What then?" said my father, "do you consider Ares a god, or only a
human passion?" And Pemptides, answering that he looked on Ares as god
of the passionate and manly element in mankind, "What," cried my father,
"shall the passionate and warlike and antagonistic instincts in man have
a god, but the affectionate and social and clubable have none? Shall
Ares, under his names of Enyalius and Stratius, preside over arms and
war and sieges and sacks of cities, and shall there be no god to witness
and preside over, to direct and guide, conjugal affection, that
friendship of closest union and communion? Why even those who hunt
gazelles and hares and deer have a silvan deity who harks and halloos
them on, for to Aristaeus[96] they pay their vows when in pitfalls and
snares they trap wolves and bears,

  'For Aristaeus first set traps for animals.'

And Hercules invoked another god, when he was about to shoot at the
bird, as the line of AEschylus shows,

  'Hunter Apollo, make my bolt go straight!'[97]

And shall no god or good genius assist and prosper the man who hunts in
the best chase of all, the chase of friendship? For I cannot for my
part, my dear Daphnaeus, consider man a less beautiful or important plant
than the oak, or sacred olive, or the vine which Homer glorifies,[98]
seeing that man too has his growth and glorious prime alike of soul and
body.""

they not Nymphs attending upon them, called Dryads, 'whose age is coeval

depravity of those he associates with? Is it not monstrous and thankless
to say so, seeing that we enjoy the divine bounty, which is dealt out to
us richly, and never abandons us in our straits? And yet some of these
same straits have more necessity than beauty. For example, our birth, in
spite of the unpleasant circumstances attending it, is witnessed by the
divine Ilithyia and Artemis: and it would be better not to be born at
all than to become bad through want of a good guardian and guide.
Moreover in sickness the god who is over that province does not desert
us, nor even in death: for even then there is a conductor and guide for
the departed, to lay them to sleep, and convey their souls to
Hades,[100] as the poet says,

  'Night bore me not to be lord of the lyre,
   Nor to be seer, or healer of diseases,
   But to conduct the souls of the departed.'

And yet these duties involve much unpleasantness, whereas we cannot
mention a holier work, nor any struggle or contest more fitting for a
god to attend and play the umpire in, than the guidance of the young and
beautiful in the prosecution of their love-affairs. For there is here
nothing of an unpleasant nature, no compulsion of any kind, but
persuasion and grace, truly making toil sweet and labour delightful,
lead the way to virtue and friendship, and do not arrive at that desired
goal without the deity, for they have as their leader and lord no other
god than Love, the companion of the Muses and Graces and Aphrodite. For
Love 'sowing in the heart of man the sweet harvest of desire,' to borrow
the language of Melanippides, mixes the sweetest and most beautiful
things together. But perhaps you are of a different opinion, Zeuxippus."

Sec. XVI. "Not I, by Zeus," replied Zeuxippus. "To have a different opinion
would be ridiculous." "Then," continued my father, "is it not also
ridiculous, if there are four kinds of friendship, for so the ancients
distinguished, the natural first, the second that to one's kindred, the
third that to one's companions, the fourth the friendship of love, and
each of the first three have a god as patron, either a god of
friendship, or a god of hospitality, or a god of the family, or a god of
the race,[101] whereas the friendship of love only, as something
altogether unholy, is left without any patron god, and that, too, when
it needs most of all attentive direction?" "It is," said Zeuxippus,
"highly ridiculous." My father continued, "The language of Plato is very
suggestive here, to make a slight digression. One kind of madness (he
says) is conveyed to the soul from the body through certain bad
temperaments or mixtures, or through the prevalence of some noxious
spirit, and is harsh, difficult to cure, and baneful. Another kind of
madness is not uninspired or from within, but an afflatus from without,
a deviation from sober reason, originated and set in motion by some
higher power, the ordinary characteristic of which is called enthusiasm.
For, as one full of breath is called [Greek: empnoos], and as one full
of sense is called [Greek: emphron], so the name enthusiasm is given to
the commotion of the soul caused by some Divine agency.[102] Thus there
is the prophetic enthusiasm which proceeds from Apollo, and the Bacchic
enthusiasm which comes from Dionysus, to which Sophocles alludes where
he says, 'Dance with the Corybantes;' for the rites of Cybele and Pan
have great affinities to the orgies of Bacchus. And the third madness
proceeds from the Muses, and possesses an impressionable and pure soul,
and stirs up the poetry and music in a man. As to the martial and
warlike madness, it is well known from what god it proceeds, namely,
Ares, 'kindling tearful war, that puts an end to the dance and the song,
and exciting civic strife.'[103] There remains, Daphnaeus, one more kind
of madness in man, neither obscure nor tranquil, as to which I should
like to ask Pemptides here,

  'What god it is that shakes the fruitful thyrsus?'

I refer to that love-fury for modest boys and chaste women, which is
far the keenest and fiercest passion of all. For have you not observed
how the soldier, when he lays aside his arms, ceases from his warlike
fury, as the poet says,

                        'Then from him
  Right gladly did his squires remove the armour,'[104]"
}

  "passage_text": "and sits down a peaceful spectator of others?[105] The Bacchic and\nCorybantic dances one can also modulate and quell, by changing the metre\nfrom the trochaic and the measure from the Phrygian. Similarly, too, the\nPythian priestess, when she descends from her tripod, possesses her soul\nin peace. Whereas the love-fury, when once it has really seized on a man\nand inflamed him, can be laid by no Muse, no charm or incantation, no\nchange of place; but present they burn, absent they desire, by day they\nfollow their loves about, by night they serenade them, sober call for\nthem, and drunken sing about them. And he who said that poetic fancies,\nowing to their vividness, were dreams of people awake, would have more\ntruly spoken so of the fancies of lovers, who, as if their loves were\npresent, converse with them, greet them, chide them. For sight seems to\npaint all other fancies on a wet ground, so soon do they fade and recede\nfrom the memory, but the images of lovers, painted by the fancy as it\nwere on encaustic tiles, leave impressions on the memory, that move, and\nlive, and speak, and are permanent for all time. The Roman Cato, indeed,\nsaid that the soul of the lover resided in the soul of the loved one,\nand I should extend the remark to the appearance, the character, the\nlife, and the actions, conducted by which he travels a long journey in a\nshort time, as the Cynics say they have found a short cut and, as it\nwere, forced march to virtue, for there is also a short cut to\nfriendship and love when the god is propitious. To sum up, the\nenthusiasm of lovers is not a thing uninspired, and the god that guides\nand governs it is none other than the god whose festival we are now\nkeeping, and to whom we are now sacrificing. Nevertheless, as we judge\nof a god mainly from his power and usefulness (as among human advantages\nwe reckon and call these two the most divine, dominion and virtue), it\nis high time to consider, before we proceed any further, whether Love\nyields to any of the gods in power. Certainly, as Sophocles says,\n'Wonderful is the power which the Cyprian Queen exerts so as always to\nwin the victory:'[106] great also is the might of Ares; and in some sort\nwe see the power of all the other gods divided among these two; for\nAphrodite has most intimate connection with the beautiful, and Ares is\nin our souls from the first to combat against the sordid, to borrow the\nidea of Plato. Let us consider, then, to begin with, that the venereal\ndelight can be purchased for six obols, and that no one ever yet put\nhimself into any trouble or danger about it, unless he was in love. And\nnot to mention here such famous courtesans as Phryne or Lais,\nGnathaenium, 'kindling her lamp at evening time,' on the look-out for\nlovers and inviting them, is often passed by; 'yet, if some sudden whiff\narise' of mighty love and desire, it makes this very delight seem equal\nto the fabled wealth of Tantalus and his domains. So feeble and cloying\nis the venereal indulgence, if Love inspires it not. And you will see\nthis more plainly still from the following consideration. Many have\nallowed others to share in their venereal enjoyments, prostituting not\nonly their mistresses but their wives, like that Roman Galba, who used\nto ask Maecenas to dinner, and when he saw from his nods and winks that\nhe had a mind to do with his wife, turned his head gently aside as if\nasleep; but when one of his slaves came up to the table and stole some\nwine, his eyes were wide open enough, and he said, 'Villain, don't you\nknow that I am asleep only for Maecenas?'[107] But this is not perhaps so\nstrange, considering Galba was a buffoon. But at Argos Nicostratus and\nPhayllus were great political rivals: so when King Philip visited that\ncity, Phayllus thought if he prostituted his wife, who was very\nhandsome, to the King, he would get from him some important office or\nplace. And Nicostratus getting wind of this, and walking about the doors\nof Phayllus' house with some of his servants on the _qui vive_,\nPhayllus made his wife put on men's boots, and a military cloak, and a\nMacedonian broad-brimmed hat, and so smuggled her into the King, without\nbeing detected, as one of the King's young men. But, of all the\nmultitude of lovers, did you ever hear of one that prostituted his\nboy-love even for the honours of Zeus? I think not. Why, though no one\nwill generally either speak or act against tyrants, many will who find\nthem their rivals and are jealous about their handsome minions. You must\nhave heard how Aristogiton of Athens, and Antileon of Metapontum, and\nMelanippus of Agrigentum, rose not against tyrants, although they saw\nhow badly they managed affairs, and what drunken tricks they played,\nyet, when they attempted the chastity of their boy-loves, they\nretaliated on them, jeoparding their lives, as if they were defending\nthe inviolability of temples and sanctuaries. It is also recorded that\nAlexander wrote to Theodoras, the brother of Proteas, 'Send me your\nsinging-girl, unless you love her yourself, and I will give you ten\ntalents;' and when Antipatridas, one of his companions, came to revel\nwith him, bringing with him a female harper, he fancied the girl not a\nlittle, and asked Antipatridas if he cared very much about her. And when\nhe replied that he did immensely, Alexander said, 'Plague take you,' but\nnevertheless abstained from touching the girl."

XVII. \"Consider also how Love excels in warlike feats, and is by no\nmeans idle, as Euripides called him,[108] nor a carpet-knight, nor\n'sleeping on a maiden's soft cheeks.'[109] For a man inspired by Love\nneeds not Ares to help him when he goes out as a warrior against the\nenemy, but at the bidding of his own god is 'ready' for his friend 'to\ngo through fire and water and whirlwinds.' And in Sophocles' play,[110]\nwhen the sons of Niobe are being shot at and dying, one of them calls\nout for no helper or assister but his lover. And you know of course how\nit was that Cleomachus the Pharsalian fell in battle?\" \"We certainly\ndon't,\" said Pemptides and those near him, \"but we should very much like\nto.\" \"Well,\" said my father, \"the tale's worth hearing. When the war\nbetween the Eretrians and Chalcidians was at its height, Cleomachus had\ncome to aid the latter with a Thessalian force; and the Chalcidian\ninfantry seemed strong enough, but they had great difficulty in\nrepelling the enemy's cavalry. So they begged that high-souled hero\nCleomachus to charge the Eretrian cavalry first. And he asked his\nboy-love, who was by, if he would be a spectator of the fight, and he\nsaying he would, and affectionately kissing him and putting his helmet\non his head, Cleomachus with a proud joy put himself at the head of the\nbravest of the Thessalians, and charged the enemy's cavalry with such\nimpetuosity that he threw them into disorder and routed them; and the\nEretrian infantry also fleeing in consequence, the Chalcidians won a\nsplendid victory. However, Cleomachus got killed, and they show his tomb\nin the market-place at Chalcis, over which a huge pillar stands to this\nday, and whereas before that the people of Chalcis had censured\nboy-loves, from that time forward they preferred that kind of love to\nthe normal love. Aristotle gives a slightly different account, namely,\nthat this Cleomachus came not from Thessaly, but from Chalcis in Thrace,\nto the help of the Chalcidians in Euboea; and that that was the origin\nof the song in vogue among the Chalcidians,\n\n  'Ye boys, who come of noble sires and beauteous are in face,\n   Grudge not to give to valiant men the joy of your embrace:\n   For Love that does the limbs relax combined with bravery\n   In the Chalcidian cities has fame that ne'er shall die.'\n\nBut according to the account of the poet Dionysius, in his\n'Causes,'[111] the name of the lover was Anton, and that of the boy-love\nwas Philistus. And among you Thebans, Pemptides, is it not usual for the\nlover to give his boy-love a complete suit of armour when he is enrolled\namong the men? And did not the erotic Pammenes change the disposition of\nthe heavy-armed infantry, censuring Homer as knowing nothing about love,\nbecause he drew up the Achaeans in order of battle in tribes and clans,\nand did not put lover and love together, that so\n\n  'Spear should be next to spear, helmet to helmet,'[112]\n\nseeing that Love is the only invincible general.[113] For men in battle\nwill leave in the lurch clansmen and friends, aye, and parents and sons,\nbut what warrior ever broke through or charged through lover and love,\nseeing that even when there is no necessity lovers frequently display\ntheir bravery and contempt of life. As Thero the Thessalian, who put his\nleft hand on a wall, and drew his sword, and chopped off his thumb, and\nchallenged his rival to do the same. And another in battle falling on\nhis face, as his enemy was about to give him the _coup-de-grace_, begged\nhim to wait a little till he could turn round, that his love should not\nsee him with a wound in his back. And not only are the most warlike\nnations most amorous, as the Boeotians the Lacedaemonians and the\nCretans, but also of the old heroes, who were more amorous than\nMeleager, Achilles, Aristomenes, Cimon, and Epaminondas. Why,\nEpaminondas had as his boy-loves Asopichus and Cephisodorus, the latter\nof whom fell with him at Mantinea, and is buried near him. As to ...,\nwho was most formidable and a source of terror to the enemy, Eucnamus of\nAmphissa, who first stood up against him and smote him, received hero\nhonours from the Phocians for his exploit. And as to all the loves of\nHercules, it would take up too much time to enumerate them, but those\nwho think that Iolaus was one of them do up to this day worship and\nhonour him, and make their loves swear fidelity at his tomb. Hercules is\nalso said, having understood the art of healing, to have preserved the\nlife of Alcestis, when she was given up by the doctors, to gratify\nAdmetus, who passionately loved his wife, and was Hercules' minion. They\nsay also in legend that Apollo was enamoured of Admetus,\n\n  'And was his hired slave for one long year.'"

For if we\nmay credit legendary lore, the stories about Alcestis, and Protesilaus,\nand Eurydice the wife of Orpheus, show that the only one of the gods\nthat Hades pays attention to is Love; although to everybody else, as\nSophocles says, \"he knows of no forbearance or favour, or anything but\nstrict justice;\" yet before lovers his genius stands rebuked, and they\nalone find him neither implacable nor relentless. Wherefore although, my\nfriend, it is an excellent thing to be initiated in the Eleusinian\nmysteries, yet I see that the votaries and initiated of Love have a\nbetter time of it in Hades than they have, * *[114] though in regard to\nlegendary lore I stand in the position of one who neither altogether\nbelieves nor altogether disbelieves. For legendary lore speaks well, and\nby a certain wonderful good fortune lights upon the truth, in saying\nthat lovers have a return from Hades to the light of day, but it knows\nnot by what way or how, having as it were got benighted on the road\nwhich Plato first discovered by philosophy. There are, indeed, some\nslender and obscure particles of truth scattered about in the mythology\nof the Egyptians, but they require a clever man to hunt them out, a man\ncapable of getting great results from small data. Wherefore let that\nmatter pass. And now next to the mighty power of Love let us consider\nits good will and favour to mankind, I do not mean as to whether it\nbestows many gifts on its votaries--that is palpable to all--but whether\nthey derive any further advantage from it. For Euripides, though very\namorous, admired a very small matter, when he wrote the line--\n\n  'Love teaches letters to a man unlearn'd.'[115]\n\nFor it makes one previously sluggish quick and intelligent, and, as has\nbeen said before, it makes the coward brave, as people harden wood in\nthe fire and make it strong from being weak. And every lover becomes\nliberal and genuine and generous, even if he was mean before, his\nlittleness and miserliness melting away like iron in the fire, so that\nthey rejoice to give to their loves more than they do to receive\nthemselves from others. You know of course that Anytus, the son of\nAnthemion, was in love with Alcibiades, and was on one occasion\nsumptuously entertaining several of his friends, when Alcibiades broke\nin and took from the table half the cups and went away again; and when\nsome of the guests were indignant and said, 'The stripling has used you\nmost insolently and contemptuously,' Anytus replied, 'Nay, rather, he\nhas dealt kindly with me, for when he might have taken all he has left\nme half.'\""

  "passage_text": "Sec. XVIII. Zeuxippus was pleased with this story, and said, \"O Hercules,\nyou have been within an ace of making me forget my hereditary hatred to\nAnytus for his behaviour to Socrates and philosophy,[116] since he was\nso mild and noble to his love.\" \"Be it so,\" said my father, \"Love also\nmakes peevish and gloomy persons kind and agreeable to those they live\nwith; for as 'when the fire blazes the house looks brighter,'[117] so\nman, it seems, becomes more cheerful through the heat of love. But most\npeople are affected rather curiously; if they see by night a light in a\nhouse, they look on it with admiration and wonder; but if they see a\nlittle, mean, and ignoble soul suddenly filled with noble-mindedness,\nfreedom, dignity, grace, and liberality, they do not feel constrained to\nsay with Telemachus, 'Surely, some god is there within.'[118] And is it\nnot wonderful, Daphnaeus,\" continued my father,[119] \"in the name of the\nGraces, that the lover who cares about hardly anything, either his\ncompanions and friends, or even the laws and magistrates and kings, who\nfears nothing, admires nothing, courts nothing, but can even endure to\ngaze on 'the forked lightning,'[120] yet directly he looks on his love\n'he crouches like a cock with drooping feathers,' and his boldness is\nbroken and his pride is cowed. And among the Muses it would not be\namiss to mention Sappho; for as the Romans say Cacus the son of\nHephaestus vomited out of his mouth fire and flames, so she really speaks\nwords that burn like fire, and in her songs shows the warmth of her\nheart, as Philoxenus puts it, 'by euphonious songs assuaging the pains\nof love.' And if you have not in your love for Lysandra forgot all your\nold love-songs, do repeat to us, Daphnaeus, the lines in which beautiful\nSappho says that 'when her love appeared her voice failed and her body\nburned, and she was seized with paleness and trembling and vertigo.'\"\nAnd when Daphnaeus had repeated the lines, my father resumed, \"In the\nname of Zeus, is not this plainly a divine seizure? Is not this a\nwonderful commotion of soul? Why, the Pythian priestess on the tripod is\nnot moved so much as this! Who of those inspired by Cybele are made\nbeside themselves to this extent by the flute and the kettledrum?\nMoreover, while many see the same body and the same beauty, only the\nlover is taken by it. Why is this the case? We get no light on it from\nMenander's words, 'Love is opportunity; and he that is smitten is the\nonly one wounded.' But the god is the cause of it, striking one and\nletting another go scot-free. But I will not pass over now, 'since it\nhas come into my mouth,' as AEschylus says, what perhaps would have been\nbetter spoken before, for it is a very important point. Perhaps, my\nfriend, of all other things which we do not perceive through the senses,\nsome got believed through legend, some through the law, some through\nreason; whereas we owe our conception of the gods altogether to the\npoets and legislators and philosophers: all alike teaching the existence\nof gods, but greatly differing as to their number and order, nature and\npower. For the gods of the philosophers 'know nothing of disease or old\nage or pain, and have not to cross the resounding Acheron;' nor do the\nphilosophers accept as gods Strifes, or Prayers, which are found in\npoetry;[121] nor will they admit Terror and Fear as gods or as the sons\nof Ares. And on many points also they are at variance with the\nlegislators, as Xenophanes bade the Egyptians, if they regarded Osiris\nas mortal, not to honour him as a god; but if they thought him a god not\nto mourn for him. And, again, the poets and legislators will not listen\nto, nor can they understand, the philosophers who make gods of ideas and\nnumbers and units and spirits. And their views generally are very\ndifferent. As there were formerly three parties at Athens, the Parali,\nthe Epacrii, and the Pediei, all at variance with one another, yet all\nagreed to vote for Solon, and chose him with one accord as their\nmediator and ruler and lawgiver, as he seemed indisputably to hold the\nfirst place in merit; so the three parties that entertain different\nviews about the gods are all unanimous on one point, for poets\nlegislators and philosophers all alike register Love as one of the gods,\n'loudly singing his praises with one voice,' as Alcaeus says the people\nof Mitylene chose Pittacus as their monarch. But our king and ruler and\ngovernor, Love, is brought down crowned from Helicon to the Academy by\nHesiod and Plato and Solon, and in royal apparel rides in a chariot\ndrawn by friendship and intimacy (not such as Euripides speaks of in the\nline, 'he has been bound in fetters not of brass,'[122] shamefully\nthrowing round him cold and heavy necessity), and soars aloft to the\nmost beautiful and divine things, about which others have spoken better\nthan I can.\""

  "passage_text": "Sec. XIX. When my father had spoken thus much, Soclarus began, "Do you see
that a second time you have committed the same fault, not cancelling
your debts as you ought to do--for I must speak my mind--but evading
them on purpose, and not delivering to us your promised ideas on a
sacred subject? For as some little time back you only just touched on
Plato and the Egyptians as if unwilling to enter on the subject more
fully, so now you are doing again. However, as to what has been
'eloquently told'[123] by Plato, or rather by the Muses through Plato's
mouth, do not tell us that, my good friend, even if we ask for it; but
as to your hint that the Egyptian legend about Love corresponded with
Plato's views, you need not discuss it fully and minutely, we shall be
satisfied if we hear a little of such mighty matters." And as the rest
of the company made the same request, my father said, "The Egyptians,
(like the Greeks) recognize two Loves, the Pandemian and the Celestial,
to which they add the Sun, they also highly venerate Aphrodite. We also
see much similarity between Love and the Sun, for neither is a fire, as
some think, but a sweet and productive radiance and warmth, the Sun
bringing to the body nourishment and light and growth, and Love doing
the same to the soul. And as the heat of the Sun is more powerful when
it emerges from clouds and after mist, so Love is sweeter and hotter
after a jealous tiff with the loved one,[124] and moreover, as some
think the Sun is kindled and extinguished, so also do people conceive of
Love as mortal and uncertain. Moreover, just as without training the
body cannot easily bear the heat of the Sun, so neither can the
untrained soul easily bear the yoke of Love, but both are equally out of
tune and suffer, for which they blame the deity and not their own
weakness. But in this respect they seem to differ, in that the Sun
exhibits to the eye things beautiful and ugly alike, whereas Love throws
its light only on beautiful things, and persuades lovers to concentrate
their attention on these, and to neglect all other things. As to those
that call Aphrodite the Moon, they, too, find some points in common
between them; for the Moon is divine and heavenly and a sort of
halfway-house between mortal and immortal, but inactive in itself and
dark without the presence of the Sun, as is the case with Aphrodite in
the absence of Love. So we may say that Aphrodite resembles the Moon,
and Love the Sun, more than any other deities, yet are not Love and the
Sun altogether the same, for just as body and soul are not the same, but
something different, so is it with the Sun and Love, the former can be
seen, the latter only felt. And if it should not seem too harsh a
saying, one might argue that the Sun acts entirely opposite to Love, for
it turns the mind away from the world of fancy to the world of reality,
beguiling us by its grace and splendid appearance, and persuading us to
seek for truth and everything else in and round it and nowhere else. For
as Euripides says,

  'Too passionately do we love the Sun,
   Because it always shines upon the earth,
   From inexperience of another life,'[125]

or rather from forgetfulness of those things which Love brings to our
remembrance. For as when we are woke by a great and bright light,
everything that the soul has seen in dreams is vanished and fled, so the
Sun is wont to banish the remembrance of past changes and chances, and
to bewitch the intelligence, pleasure and admiration causing this
forgetfulness. And though reality is really there, yet the soul cleaves
to dreams and is dazzled by what is most beautiful and divine. 'For
round the soul are poured sweet yet deceiving dreams,' so that the soul
thinks everything here good and valuable, unless it obtain divine and
chaste Love as its physician and preserver. For Love brings the soul
through the body to truth and the region of truth, where pure and
guileless beauty is to be found, kindly befriending its votaries like an
initiator at the mysteries. And it associates with the soul only through
the body. And as geometricians, in the case of boys who cannot yet be
initiated into the perception of incorporeal and impassive substance,
convey their ideas through the medium of spheres, cubes, and
dodecahedrons, so celestial Love has contrived beautiful mirrors of
beautiful things, and exhibits them to us glittering in the shapes
colours and appearances of youths in all their flower, and calmly stirs
the memory which is inflamed first by these. Consequently some, through
the stupidity of their friends and intimates, who have endeavoured by
force and against reason to extinguish the flame, have got no advantage
from it, but filled themselves with smoke and confusion, or have rushed
into secret and lawless pleasures and ingloriously wasted their prime.
But as many as by sober reason and modesty have abated the extravagance
of the passion, and left in the soul only a bright glow--not exciting a
tornado of passion, but a wonderful and productive diffusion, as in a
growing plant, opening the pores of complaisance and friendliness--these
in no long time cease to regard the personal charms of those they love,
and study their inward characters, and gaze at one another with
unveiled eyes, and associate with one another in words and actions, if
they find in their minds any fragment or image of the beautiful; and if
not they bid them farewell and turn to others, like bees that only go to
those flowers from which they can get honey. But wherever they find any
trace or emanation or pleasing resemblance of the divine, in an ecstasy
of pleasure and delight they indulge their memory, and revive to
whatever is truly lovely and felicitous and admired by everybody.""
}

XX. \"The poets indeed seem for the most part to have written and sung\nabout Love in a playful and merry manner, but have sometimes spoken\nseriously about him, whether out of their own mind, or the god helping\nthem to truth. Among these are the lines about his birth,\n'Well-sandalled Iris bare the most powerful of the gods to golden-haired\nZephyr.'[126] But perhaps the learned have persuaded you that these\nlines are only a fanciful illustration of the variety and beauty of\nlove.\" \"Certainly,\" said Daphnaeus, \"what else could they mean?\" \"Hear\nme,\" said my father, \"for the heavenly phenomenon compels us so to\nspeak. The rainbow[127] is, I suppose, a reflection caused by the sun's\nrays falling on a moist cloud, making us think the appearance is in the\ncloud. Similarly erotic fancy in the case of noble souls causes a\nreflection of the memory, from things which here appear and are called\nbeautiful, to what is really divine and lovely and felicitous and\nwonderful. But most lovers pursuing and groping after the semblance of\nbeauty in boys and women, as in mirrors,[128] can derive nothing more\ncertain than pleasure mixed with pain. And this seems the love-delirium\nof Ixion, who instead of the joy he desired embraced only a cloud, as\nchildren who desire to take the rainbow into their hands, clutching at\nwhatever they see. But different is the behaviour of the noble and\nchaste lover: for he reflects on the divine beauty that can only be\nfelt, while he uses the beauty of the visible body only as an organ of\nthe memory, though he embraces it and loves it, and associating with it\nis still more inflamed in mind. And so neither in the body do they sit\never gazing at and desiring this light, nor after death do they return\nto this world again, and skulk and loiter about the doors and\nbedchambers of newly-married people, disagreeable ghosts of\npleasure-loving and sensual men and women, who do not rightly deserve\nthe name of lovers. For the true lover, when he has got into the other\nworld and associated with beauties as much as is lawful, has wings and\nis initiated and passes his time above in the presence of his Deity,\ndancing and waiting upon him, until he goes back to the meadows of the\nMoon and Aphrodite, and sleeping there commences a new existence. But\nthis is a subject too high for the present occasion. However, it is with\nLove as with the other gods, to borrow the words of Euripides, 'he\nrejoices in being honoured by mankind,'[129] and _vice versa_, for he is\nmost propitious to those that receive him properly, but visits his\ndispleasure on those that affront him. For neither does Zeus as god of\nHospitality punish and avenge any outrages on strangers or suppliants,\nnor as god of the family fulfil the curses of parents, as quickly as\nLove hearkens to lovers unfairly treated, being the chastiser of boorish\nand haughty persons. Why need I mention the story of Euxynthetus and\nLeucomantis, the latter of whom is called The Peeping Girl to this day\nin Cyprus? But perhaps you have not heard of the punishment of the\nCretan Gorgo, a somewhat similar case to that of Leucomantis, except\nthat she was turned into stone as she peeped out of window to see her\nlover carried out to burial. For this Gorgo had a lover called Asander,\na proper young man and of a good family, but reduced in fortune, though\nhe thought himself worthy to mate with anybody. So he wooed Gorgo, being\na relation of hers, and though he had many rivals, as she was much run\nafter for her wealth belike, yet he had won the esteem of all the\nguardians and relations of the young girl.[130] * * * *\n\nSec. XXI. * * * Now the origins and causes of Love are not peculiar to\neither sex, but common to both. For those attractions that make men\namorous may as well proceed from women as from boys.[131] And as to\nthose beautiful and holy reminiscences and invitations to the divine and\ngenuine and Olympian beauty, by which the soul soars aloft, what hinders\nbut that they may come either from boys or lads, maidens or grown women,\nwhenever a chaste and orderly nature and beauteous prime are associated\ntogether (just as a neat shoe exhibits the shapeliness of the foot, to\nborrow the illustration of Aristo), whenever connoisseurs of beauty\ndescry in beautiful forms and pure bodies clear traces of an upright and\nunenervated soul.[132] For if[133] the man of pleasure, who was asked\nwhether \"he was most given to the love of women or boys,\" and answered,\n\"I care not which so beauty be but there,\" is considered to have given\nan appropriate answer as to his erotic desires, shall the noble lover of\nbeauty neglect beauty and nobility of nature, and make love only with an\neye to the sexual parts? Why, the lover of horses will take just as much\npleasure in the good points of Podargus, as in those of AEthe,\nAgamemnon's mare,[134] and the sportsman rejoices not only in dogs, but\nalso rears Cretan and Spartan bitches,[135] and shall the lover of the\nbeautiful and of humanity be unfair and deal unequally with either sex,\nand think that the difference between the loves of boys and women is\nonly their different dress? And yet they say that beauty is a flower of\nvirtue; and it is ridiculous to assert that the female sex never\nblossoms nor make a goodly show of virtue, for as AEschylus truly says,\n\n  'I never can mistake the burning eye\n   Of the young woman that has once known man.'[136]"
